10020-the-strand-magazine-vol-07-issue-3:
The Strand Magazine for January 1894, volume seven, issue thirty-seven, edited by George Newnes, opens its contents with Stories from the Diary of a Doctor. The seventh tale, The Horror of Studley Grange, comes from the authors of The Medicine Lady.

Other pieces include The Queen of Holland by Mary Spencer-Warren and Zig-Zags at the Zoo, nineteenth in the series, on the batrachian, by A. G. Morrison. The Strand's illustrated monthly format made it the home of popular fiction. Readers get a crisp sample of 1890s magazine entertainment, in pictures and prose.
10992-cleopatra:
Jacob Abbott wrote this young readers' history of Cleopatra as part of his Makers of History series. Chapters begin with the Nile valley, the Ptolemies, and Alexandria, then follow Cleopatra's father, her accession, and her relations with Caesar and Antony. Battles at Philippi and Actium lead to her end, with illustrations including her testing poison on slaves.

Abbott frames the story as a moral tale about unlawful love and its ruin, a view modern readers will find dated. Yet his clear narrative explains Egyptian geography, the Nile flood, and Alexandria's founding along the way. The book works as an introduction to ancient history for younger readers, and as a period example of how Victorians told famous lives.
11047-libro-segundo-de-lectura:
Ellen M. Cyr wrote this second Spanish-English reader for young learners, pairing short Spanish passages with English versions and word lists. A girl named Louise shows her new doll to her grandfather on a holiday, worries that the doll has no hat and will catch cold, and plays with Mary. Rain fairies and sun fairies explain the rainbow.

Each lesson teaches a few words at a time, with pronunciation help, so children learn Spanish through stories about dolls, carriages made from dustpans, and sweets bought for a cent. The book suits beginners, teachers, and families learning Spanish together, and it shows early bilingual teaching methods, simple, repetitive, and rooted in a child's daily life.
11050-taquisara:
F. Marion Crawford wrote this 1895 Italian romance about Veronica Serra, a young princess of Acireale, who signs her will before a Neapolitan notary, Lamberto Squarci. Her aunt and uncle, Count and Countess Macomer, watch eagerly as she writes, while a clerk waits to witness. An ink blot, blotted with pink paper, delays the signing for a moment.

Poison, pain, and a faithful servant named Elettra soon darken the story, as Gregorio howls in his room and Matilde warns him to hide the truth. Crawford builds a plot of inheritance, family greed, and a young woman's peril in Sicilian high society. The novel mixes romance with suspense, and it shows Crawford's skill at Italian settings and tangled family intrigue.
1130-antony-and-cleopatra:
Mark Antony, Rome's great soldier, abandons duty for Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt, and their love affair drags the Roman world into civil war. William Shakespeare's tragedy sweeps from Alexandria to Rome to the sea battle of Actium, where Antony's fleet flees and his fate seals.

Cleopatra, witty, regal, and changeable, dominates the play, and Antony's ruin is both political and personal. Octavius's cold triumph closes the tale. The play's verse is rich and swift, and its lovers remain the most glamorous pair in Shakespeare. Their love affair remains the most glamorous in all of Shakespeare.
12019-queen-hortense-a-life-picture-of-t:
L. Mühlbach's Queen Hortense, a life picture of the Napoleonic era, translated from German by Chapman Coleman and published in 1910, follows Hortense de Beauharnais from childhood to queenship. Mühlbach, author of Prince Eugene and His Times, Joseph II and His Court, and Merchant of Berlin, writes popular historical biography as melodrama.

Book 1 covers days of childhood and of the revolution, with chapters on a prophecy, the consequences of the revolution, General Bonaparte, and the marriage that tied Hortense's family to Napoleon. The life picture method lets Mühlbach move between nursery, salon, and battlefield, showing how a woman's private fortunes were caught in the revolutions and empires of her time.
13369-the-lost-ambassador-or-the-search-:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's 1910 thriller follows the search for Delora, a missing woman at the centre of Paris cafés, dinners, and dangerous play. The narrator meets her, loses her, and chases her through telephone calls, double assignations, and an informal tribunal, with Louis, the maître d'hôtel, explaining more than he seems to know.

Felicia Delora, a dangerous impersonation, wheels within wheels, and a terrible night raise the stakes. Oppenheim keeps the action in hotels, restaurants, and drawing rooms, where a voice on the telephone or a guest at dinner can change everything. It is an Edwardian society mystery built on charm, secrecy, and a woman who will not stay found.
13459-the-waters-of-edera:
Ouida's 1900 novel The Waters of Edera opens in a wide, sparse country of pastures, moors, rock-born streams, and forest, with the sea eastward unseen and mountains always in view. Herdsmen, shepherds, pedlars, and pack mules cross almost disused roads, while minerals and marbles lie unsought under turf and temple ruins grow over with weeds.

A man ponders for days, then rides the arduous road to San Beda, a small mountain city on marble rocks, old as Ruscino and fortified like a monastery. Clelia, who brings her conscience to his judgment, argues against wrongs the weak must bear, like teal against sportsmen's guns. Ouida writes a romance of a valley, its people, and the powers that press upon them.
13723-leonora:
Arnold Bennett set this 1903 novel in the Potteries town of Bursley, here called Hillport. Leonora, a proud and restless woman, watches her marriage and social world with sharp eyes. Meshach and Hannah, comic opera, a dance, and a death in the family mark the chapters. A trip to London tests Leonora's choices.

Bennett studies class, money, and marriage with dry wit. Leonora's charm and vanity pull against duty and affection. Ethel, younger and simpler, forms a contrast that sharpens the portrait. The novel moves between drawing rooms, theatres, and town streets. It shows Bennett's early skill at social observation. Leonora remains a lively, flawed heroine.
13967-nedra:
George Barr McCutcheon published Nedra in 1906, a romance of flight, Manila, and mistaken identity. Mr. Ridge and Miss Ridge sail for Manila, with Henry Veath and a beautiful stranger aboard. Glum days, a sharp encounter, and a discovery follow. The Harlequin's tale and later chapters deepen the mystery.

Hugh and Grace argue over a wedding dictated by a twice-married relative. Grace defends the older woman's love, while Hugh resents interference. McCutcheon, author of Brewster's Millions, writes with his usual wit and pace. Illustrations by Harrison Fisher add glamour. The novel suits fans of early twentieth-century romantic adventure.
1479-a-vanished-arcadia-being-some-accou:
R. B. Cunninghame Graham's short history tells of the Jesuit missions of Paraguay from 1607 to 1767, where priests built ordered towns for the Guarani people, with farms, workshops, and churches run in common. For a century and a half these reductions stood apart from the slave trade around them.

Graham traces their rise, their clash with settlers and crowns, and their fall when the Jesuits were expelled and the towns broke up. His tone is admiring and elegiac. The book offers a vivid, if romantic, account of a bold social experiment and the world that destroyed it.
15118-the-narrative-of-lunsford-lane-for:
Lunsford Lane, formerly enslaved at Raleigh, North Carolina, published this narrative at Boston in 1842. He tells how he bought his own freedom and that of his family. He was then banished from his birthplace for the crime, as the title puts it, of wearing a colored skin. A mother's poem to her infant child opens the book.

Lane writes with plain dignity about work, purchase, and exile, and about a system that punished free Black people for being free. The narrative is short but pointed, and it served the abolition cause in its day. It remains a clear, firsthand witness to slavery, self-purchase, and the harsh limits placed on Black freedom.
1534-antony-and-cleopatra:
Shakespeare's great Roman tragedy follows Mark Antony, torn between Rome and Egypt, duty and love. In Alexandria he lingers with Cleopatra, queen of charm and politics, while Octavius Caesar gathers power in Rome; war follows, and Antony's fleet deserts him at Actium.

From Alexandria to Rome and back, the play moves with epic sweep, and its language is among Shakespeare's richest. Antony dies in Cleopatra's arms, and she dies by her own hand rather than grace Caesar's triumph. It is a tragedy of empire, passion, and two larger-than-life lovers.
16768-the-history-of-sumatra:
William Marsden wrote this history of Sumatra, third edition with corrections, additions, and plates, printed in London in 1811. It gives the government, laws, customs, and manners of the native peoples, with a description of natural products and a relation of the island's ancient political state. Chapters take up land, lakes, rivers, monsoons, volcanoes, quakes, villages, food, and rice farming.

Marsden writes as a scholar who lived with his topic, ordering a vast island by topic rather than by tale. His plates, including a Malay boy of Bencoolen, add to the text. The book remains a key early source on Sumatra, valued for its breadth and its detail, though modern readers will read its colonial views with care.
16840-stories-of-the-wagner-opera:
H. A. Guerber wrote this 1905 book of Wagner opera stories, issued by Dodd, Mead in New York, with copyright in 1895. Her preface says these short sketches, readable in a few moments, aim to give as clear an outline as possible of the great dramatist-composer's work. Contents run from Rienzi and the Flying Dutchman, through Tannhauser, Lohengrin, Tristan, and the Mastersingers, to the Ring cycle and Parsifal.

Guerber retells each opera's plot in plain prose, with verse quotes credited to helpers and publishers. Her sketches help a first-time listener follow long, complex works. The book gives a friendly, old-style guide to Wagner, best used before a hearing or a first visit to the opera house.
175-the-phantom-of-the-opera:
Beneath the Paris Opera lives a masked figure who tutors a young singer and haunts box five. Gaston Leroux's Phantom of the Opera follows Christine Daaé as the voice she calls the Angel of Music draws her below the stage. Raoul, her childhood love, seeks to save her.

The Persian, a shadowy witness, guides Raoul through trapdoors, torture chambers, and a lake beneath the theater. Leroux frames the tale as a true investigation, with footnotes and documents. The phantom's love, rage, and ugliness drive the horror. The novel inspired the famous musical and many films.
17843-the-mysterious-shin-shira:
G. E. Farrow wrote The Mysterious Shin Shira, printed in London by Henry Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton, with pictures by W. G. Easton. Farrow, author of The Wallypug of Why, here gives children ten short mysteries, each a small wonder in itself.

Shin Shira appears, meets a dragon, and rides a magic carpet. He charms a duchess, aids a lame duck, and finds a diamond. He faces a roc and a mad bull, meets the Queen of Hearts, and then vanishes. The tales are brief, fanciful, and full of color, best read one mystery at a time.
18183-trees-fruits-and-flowers-of-minnes:
A. W. Latham edited Trees, Fruits and Flowers of Minnesota, 1916, embracing the transactions of the Minnesota State Horticultural Society from December 1915 to December 1916. The volume, number forty-four, joins the twelve numbers of The Minnesota Horticulturist for that year.

Its pages greet the forty-ninth annual meeting, note a monument of twenty-five bushels of apples in a Minneapolis hotel lobby, and share growers' trials with trees, fruits, and flowers. Latham warns that each piece gives its writer's own experience, to be weighed as such. It is a rich farm record of Minnesota growing, full of practical notes for cold-climate gardeners.
18547-madame-flirt-a-romance-of-the-begg:
Charles E. Pearce wrote this historical romance, first published in 1922 by Stanley Paul in London, as a romance of The Beggar's Opera. The opening places a portly man and his sleeping friend in the bow window of the Maiden Head Inn in St. Giles, watching a pretty girl and calling her Polly.

The novel draws its characters and its air from John Gay's opera world of thieves, beggars, and fine talk in eighteenth-century London. Pearce, author of stirring war tales and romances, sets love and roguery side by side, letting the opera's songs and low London life carry the story.
18562-outlines-of-the-earth-s-history-a-:
Nathaniel Southgate Shaler, Harvard geology professor, wrote this popular study of physiography, published at New York and London in 1898 with a 1910 printing. Aimed at beginners, it explains the earth's history through forces still at work, rather than as a finished past. Shaler stresses the heat of the sun driving air and water, and warns against the old static view of the earth.

He also shows how geology shaped human fate, calling the earth the well-appointed nursery of our kind. Pictures, including dunes at Ipswich Light, aid the text. The book remains a clear, friendly entry to earth science for new readers.
1873-gambara:
By a fire in a retreat overlooking Paris, a narrator hears about Gambara, a composer whose music no one can bear to hear and who believes himself a genius. The dedication to the Marquis de Belloy frames a tale told beside a fire in a retreat above Paris, where the narrator's eyes command the city from the heights.

Marcosini, a listener, marvels that all the world knows Mozart, author of Don Giovanni and the Requiem. Gambara's name is unknown, and the story turns on the cruelty of that gap. Balzac writes about art and madness with sympathy, and the novella's sadness comes from a man who hears harmonies no one else can hear.
18782-studies-in-song-a-century-of-round:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Studies in Song, A Century of Roundels, Sonnets on English Dramatic Poets, and The Heptalogia appear here from volume five of his collected poetical works. The volume was published at London by Heinemann in 1917, first printed by Chatto in 1904. The contents open with Athens, an ode praising the free spirit of Greece, then a statue poem for Victor Hugo and lines on Trelawny's death.

Child poems follow, with a child's pity, laughter, thanks, battles, and future, beside odes, elegies, and the closing Sunrise. Roundels and sonnets on dramatists show Swinburne's formal skill. The volume gives a rich mid-career sample of his lyric and formal verse.
19307-the-lion-of-petra:
Talbot Mundy wrote this tale of Petra, opening with a warning that it is not an animal story. No four-legged lions live at Petra now, he says, since biped lions outdid them, though Assyrian kings once hunted real yellow cats there and bragged after. The Lion of the title is a man.

Riders cross bone-dry hills above the Dead Sea valley, where heat rises like fumes from white-hot charcoal, and reach Hebron in dust to meet the governor de Crespigny. Ali Higg, camels, and aeroplanes fill later chapters. Readers get a vivid desert adventure of intrigue, wit, and a lion among men.
19958-some-forerunners-of-italian-opera:
W. J. Henderson's Some Forerunners of Italian Opera, dated 1911, traces opera before opera. Egyptians sang jubilations to their gods, he begins. Those were florid cadences on prolonged vowel sounds. Greeks likewise caroled on vowels in honor of their deities. Such singing is older than the Christian era's foundations. Henderson builds a long runway toward Florence, where opera was born.

Henderson was the New York Sun's formidable music critic. His history honors the madrigalists and early experimenters. Monody, the sung speech of 1600, is his destination. Forerunners matter because opera claims a sudden birth. Henderson proves a long gestation instead. The book remains a readable doorway into opera's prehistory.
20264-parsifal-story-and-analysis-of-wag:
H. R. Haweis wrote Parsifal, a story and analysis of Wagner's great opera. Haweis recalls walking toward the festival through Wagner's own Bayreuth grounds. Pale petals of wild roses scatter upon his path as he goes. A stream of people moves down the avenue by the Neue Schloss.

Parsifal was Wagner's last opera, a sacred tale of the Holy Grail. Haweis retells its plot and then weighs its music and meaning. He writes for newcomers who want a guide before they listen. Readers get a warm, period doorway into Wagner's most solemn work.
21472-ned-garth-or-made-prisoner-in-afri:
Ned Garth watches a strange craft off the coast at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's Ned Garth. His uncle, Lieutenant John Pack, has lost a leg and walks with a thick stick. The two had been out on an errand of mercy to an injured fisherman.

The tale carries Ned to Africa, where he is made prisoner, as the subtitle says. Kingston aims the book squarely at the horrors of the slave trade. Sea scenes, capture, and the fight against slaving fill the action. Ned's sharp young eyes, keener than his uncle's, serve him well when danger comes close.
21907-an-investigation-into-the-nature-o:
Coal dust kills slowly in Archibald Makellar's investigation of black phthisis, reprinted at Edinburgh in 1846 from a medical journal. Makellar, a fellow of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh, read his findings to the Medico-Chirurgical Society in July 1845. He studied the East Lothian coal miners in particular. As the disease advances, he writes, the heart grows feeble and the blood shows a dark, carbon-like mixing.

The cause, he argues, is breathed-in filth: gunpowder smoke, lamp smoke, and dust hanging in badly aired pits. His name for it, ulceration from carbon gathered in the lungs, describes black lung disease exactly. The paper is an early landmark of workplace medicine. It gave miners' suffering a cause, a course, and a doctor's sworn witness.
2268-antony-and-cleopatra:
Mark Antony, torn between Rome and Egypt, loves Cleopatra even as Octavius Caesar tightens his grip on the world. Antony and Cleopatra sweeps from Alexandria's feasts to Actium's sea battle, following a passion that undoes an empire. Shakespeare gives Cleopatra infinite variety: witty, jealous, theatrical, and finally majestic in death.

Enobarbus, Antony's loyal soldier, deserts and dies of shame, a small tragedy inside the large one. The lovers' suicides close the play with grandeur rather than despair. Readers meet Shakespeare's most worldly tragedy, vast in geography and feeling. Octavius, the cold young Caesar, serves as a foil to Antony's warmth throughout.
22834-voyage-of-h-m-s-pandora:
A forgotten manuscript drives Voyage of H.M.S. Pandora. For more than a century, the editor notes, an account written by one of the main actors in the drama sat unread in the Record Office. The Pandora's mission gives that drama its shape. The frigate sailed to Tahiti to seize the Bounty mutineers.

The narrative follows the hunt, the capture, and the disastrous wreck on the return voyage. Prisoners in irons, a sinking ship, and open-boat escapes supply grim incident, all told from inside the expedition. Few naval stories mix triumph and horror so closely. This printing rescued a firsthand record from the archive, and it remains a key source on the Bounty affair.
22965-ten-thousand-miles-with-a-dog-sled:
Hudson Stuck measures Alaska's scale in Ten Thousand Miles with a Dog Sled, his narrative of winter travel in the interior. Alaska, he warns, is not one country at all. The territory arcs across huge spans of latitude and longitude. In climate, population, resources, and daily needs, it behaves like four or five separate lands.

Stuck, an Episcopal archdeacon, traveled his vast parish by dog team, and the book records missions, villages, cold, and dogs with equal care. Few travel books cover so much hard ground so plainly. His respect for Native Alaskans and for his teams sets the tone. The narrative stands as a classic of northern travel, written from the trail rather than about it.
2299-pandora:
Henry James sends his heroine Pandora Day across the Atlantic in this sharp little tale of American manners. Pandora is a bright, self-made young woman from a modest background. She meets an American diplomat aboard a North German Lloyd steamer and later in Washington society, where her push and candor scandalize the old guard. James watches the social game with cool amusement.

The story turns on whether Pandora's energy is vulgarity or the future, and James leaves the verdict open. Its portraits of expatriates and climbers are precise and funny. Readers of James will enjoy this compact, sparkling novella.
23399-little-white-barbara:
Eleanor S. March wrote and pictured this Dumpy Book for Children, printed in London in nineteen hundred two. Little White Barbara earns her name from her very white face, and she lives with two kind aunts, Aunt Dosy and Aunt Posy.

The aunts talk all day about what Barbara ought to do and wear, fussing over her with fond care. Short lines and bright colour pictures carry each small scene, so a tiny child can follow the story picture by picture. The book charms through its gentle humour and its cosy household, a small world where aunts rule, a little girl listens, and kindness wins the day.
23930-beyond-pandora:
Robert J. Martin's Beyond Pandora opens in a doctor's office, where a patient reports his third set of teeth, slow in coming. Last year he lost a thumb in a stupid accident. Regrowth took nearly half a year, and the doctor calls that much too long.

Tissue regeneration, the doctor says, is pretty well under control, and the man is due for another booster, with the usual tests. The story's motto states its theme: turn any menace to use. Martin's future is one of regrown thumbs, booster shots, and careful records, where medicine has made the body almost too repairable.
2421-the-beggar-s-opera:
John Gay's Beggar's Opera turns opera upside down: beggars and thieves sing ballads in Newgate, and the highwayman Macheath juggles two lovers, Polly Peachum and Lucy Lockit. Gay's 1728 ballad opera satirizes Italian opera, corrupt politicians, and polite society all at once, with thieves behaving like ministers and ministers like thieves. The songs, set to popular tunes, made it a sensation.

The work invented English musical theater's satirical tradition and still plays well. Its wit is sharp, its targets recognizable, and its hero roguishly charming. Theater lovers will find a foundational, funny classic.
24427-princess-zara:
Ross Beeckman wrote this novel, with pictures by Bert Knight, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in January 1909, copyrighted in 1908 and 1909 by W. J. Watt and Company. Its frontispiece carries the line, I do love you. Its theme verse by Susan Marr Spalding tells of two born the whole wide world apart, speaking different tongues, with no thought of each other's being.

Over unknown seas to unknown lands they cross, escaping wreck and defying death. They shape every act toward one end, that one day, out of darkness, they shall meet and read life's meaning in each other's eyes. Chapters run from a lady of quality and a warning through Dan Derrington's story, the presence of the czar, and a nihilist spy. The princess' oriental garden, a secret interview, and sentenced to death follow. Readers get a romance of czars, spies, and fate.
24700-a-history-of-french-literature-sho:
Edward Dowden, professor of English literature at Dublin, wrote this history of French literature, published at London in 1914 by William Heinemann, with a first edition in 1897. It belongs to the Short Histories of the Literatures of the World, edited by Edmund Gosse. Dowden's first book covers the Middle Ages.

Chapters treat narrative religious poetry, the national epic, romances of love and courtesy, lyrical poetry, Renard the Fox, fabliaux, and the Romance of the Rose. Later books carry the story to modern times. Students will find Dowden's history clear, learned, and readable, a classic survey of French letters.
25418-the-baby-s-opera:
Walter Crane's Baby's Opera, a book of old rhymes with new dresses, sets nursery songs to music by the earliest masters. Engraved and printed in colors by Edmund Evans for Frederick Warne, it pairs Crane's pictures with songs children still sing.

Rhymes include Girls and Boys, King Cole, and Jack and Jill, with the frog and the crow in a full song sequence. Lyrics from the music notation tell how a jolly fat frog met a comely black crow, danced in yellow, and parted company by the lake. The book, dedicated to Mrs. George Howard, is a Victorian nursery treasure.
2631-mr-gladstone-and-genesis-essay-5-fr:
Thomas Henry Huxley takes on William Gladstone in this essay on Genesis, opening with a courtship rule: be off with the old before you are on with the new. Huxley applies the rule to Gladstone's attempt to reconcile the first chapters of Genesis with modern science.

He sifts Gladstone's arguments cloud by cloud, asking what they actually prove and where they beg the question. The prose is urbane but unsparing, and the essay shows Huxley at his polemical best. Readers get a Victorian clash between science and scripture, fought with logic, humor, and very little mercy.
26379-vice-in-its-proper-shape-or-the-wo:
Printed at Worcester, Massachusetts, by Isaiah Thomas in 1789, this children's book warns good boys and girls against bad conduct. It turns naughty masters and misses into the beasts they most resemble in temper. Its introduction borrows the old doctrine of Pythagoras, that souls after death pass into other bodies, even those of beasts, birds, or insects, according to their prior behavior.

A tale of the East Indies illustrates the notion, where a man who shot a heron faced prosecution from a native who held the bird housed his father's soul. The stories that follow show faults repaid in fitting animal shape, including Stephen, flogged by his master, who runs away and joins gypsies, supping on roasted cat. The moral is plain: character shows, and ill conduct degrades.
2723-a-first-family-of-tasajara:
Bret Harte opens this novel with wind shaking the long wooden store at Sidon settlement in Contra Costa. Joe Wingate notes that it blows, and a whistle through keyholes and glass doors fills the building as the story gathers.

A first family of Tasajara, proud, ruined, and scheming, fights for standing in a new California town. Harte mixes land hunger, love, and social climbing with his usual irony. The novel offers a compact drama of a family inventing itself, and of a state inventing itself beside them. Wind shakes the store as surely as pride shakes the family.
2769-cleopatra:
H. Rider Haggard dedicated this romance of Cleopatra to his mother, hoping she would accept it despite its shortcomings and whatever judgment others passed. The queen of Egypt, he trusted, would earn a mother's indulgence as well as a reader's attention.

Cleopatra moves through love, war, and the fall of a kingdom, with Antony, Caesar, and the gods of the Nile around her. Haggard writes with grandeur and romance, in the manner of his African tales transplanted to Egypt. The novel offers a sweeping portrait of history's most famous queen.
27906-the-voyage-of-the-aurora:
Harry Collingwood wrote The Voyage of the Aurora, opening with Lucy Walford and the little village of Alverstoke near Gosport, about a mile from town and half a mile from the Solent. In the year the history opens, Alverstoke was unimportant to the public but very important to His Majesty's Customs.

Its inhabitants, almost to a man, had added smuggling to fishing and market-gardening, to the great loss of the king's revenues. The village street, churchyard, cottages, and public houses set the scene for a seafaring adventure of smugglers, customs men, and a voyage, in Collingwood's reliable manner.
27980-wood-rangers-the-trappers-of-sonor:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote Wood Rangers, the trappers of Sonora, opening with Pepe the sleeper and the little Biscayan village of Elanchovi, set in an amphitheatre of cliffs above a stone jetty. The village street climbs like a stairway past fishermen's houses to an old chateau of the Mediana family.

In 1808, during the French invasion, Count Don Juan made the chateau a safe residence for his wife Doña Luisa, loved also by his younger brother Don Antonio, who left in anger. The novel follows trappers, rivalry, and adventure from Spain to Sonora, in Reid's romantic frontier manner.
28-the-fables-of-aesop-selected-told-ane:
Joseph Jacobs retold the classic animal fables for a new generation in 1894. His Aesop volume pairs each tale with pictures by Richard Heighway. A short history traces how the fables traveled from ancient sources to modern books.

Familiar tales appear here: the wolf and the lamb, the town mouse and the country mouse, the fox and the crow. The lion and the mouse, the ant and the grasshopper, and the wolf in sheep's clothing follow. Each tale ends with a plain moral on greed, pride, or kindness. The volume suits readers meeting Aesop for the first time.
28102-the-transfiguration-of-miss-philur:
Florence Morse Kingsley's The Transfiguration of Miss Philura, thirteenth edition, 1901, is a short novel of a New England spinster. Miss Philura Rice, faded and wistful, ties her bonnet and studies her face in a cousin's mirror, wondering at a life that has grown narrow. Her scant eyebrows, once helped by burnt match, stand for years of quiet hopes.

A new teaching on thought forces and the infinite reaches her, and Philura begins to change in mind and manner. Kingsley tells the change with humour and warmth, not scorn. The novel offers a kind, comic portrait of a woman remaking herself late in life.
28398-movement-of-the-international-lite:
Movement of the International Literary Exchanges between France and North America, published in Paris in 1846, records a scientific exchange scheme from January 1845 to May 1846. Professors and administrators of the Museum of Natural History at Paris describe how books, specimens, and publications passed between France and America.

The volume prints official documents at the request of young Americans then in Paris, led by Benjamin Perley Poore, who thanked the museum for its disinterested toil. It also gives instructions for collecting, preparing, and forwarding objects of natural history, with guidance on anthropology and zoology by Isidore Geoffroy St-Hilaire. Both series were translated by an American lady.
28609-the-cornish-riviera:
Sidney Heath's The Cornish Riviera, pictured by E. W. Haslehust for Blackie and Son, runs from Plymouth to Land's End. The volume belongs to the Beautiful England series, and its pictures include Fowey Harbour, Truro Cathedral, Falmouth, St. Michael's Mount, Penzance, Newlyn, and Land's End. Heath opens with the old saying: by Tre, Pol, and Pen, you may know the Cornishmen.

Cornwall, he argues, lacks the cathedrals, spas, and physical beauty that draw tourists elsewhere, coast excepted. Instead it offers Celtic saints, crosses, holy wells, history, legend, and folklore in abundance. Until recent years few tourists came, and natives spoke of England as a foreign country. Readers get a coastal county, modest and storied.
29096-memoranda-sacra:
J. Rendel Harris wrote this devotional book, Memoranda Sacra, in a fourth edition published by Hodder and Stoughton in London in 1907. Harris dedicates it to beloved friends in Christ Jesus, recalling Cambridge meetings for worship and personal help, when pencilled notes passed from hand to hand to be copied and circulated. The papers were gathered over more than fourteen years, and the latest fragment is more than ten years old.

The contents run through God the God of the living, believing and becoming, gleaming as crystal, heart enlargement, and he restoreth my soul. A closing conference treats death and tests of faith, love, and rightness. Readers get a quiet, affectionate volume of Christian meditation, written to keep friends in remembrance of one another and of truths God taught them.
29542-the-valor-of-cappen-varra:
Poul Anderson's tale of Cappen Varra draws on legend from the northern countries, where the pagan past seems only like yesterday. The story opens with Torbek of Norren squinting into the night, his leathery face a mesh of wrinkles, calling the feast bitter and the voyage madness. Wind from the north drives sleet and spindrift as a ship lurches through winter night, with waves rushing and clamoring beyond the rail.

Cappen, a little singer, is urged to go: perhaps his songs can lull the trolls. Anderson turns a northern legend into a fantasy of courage, song, and strange shadows surviving from dim pasts. Fans of Anderson and of Norse-flavored fantasy will enjoy a vivid, windswept tale of a small hero.
29911-the-strand-magazine-vol-05-issue-2:
The Strand Magazine, volume five, issue twenty-five, is dated January 1893. George Newnes edited the illustrated monthly in London. Its opening tale in this issue is Shafts from an Eastern Quiver, part seven, by Charles J. Mansford. The tale is called Margarita, the Bond Queen of the Wandering Dhahs, and its front picture bears the oath We Swear.

Hassan tells Denviers that the Cingalese call the queen of the Dhahs a Sahibmem, an Englishwoman. Denviers doubts that any civilized being would reign over so queer a race. An indolent native interrupts to say he saw her himself. The travellers have crossed from Southern India to Ceylon, stayed at Colombo, and struck inland toward Kandi. The tale is a brisk imperial adventure in the Strand style.
3010-the-vicomte-de-bragelonne-the-end-a:
Alexandre Dumas's Vicomte de Bragelonne, the final D'Artagnan romance, appears here with framing material by John Bursey. The introduction contrasts this novel with The Three Musketeers and Twenty Years After, where four heroes battled evil with swordplay, bravado, ingenuity, and great fortune. Their cry, all for one and one for all, has echoed for a century and a half through films, commercials, and even a candy bar.

Bursey warns that the Vicomte is a different sort of novel, sadder and more reflective, with flaws in history and chronology that readers have forgiven for generations. The musketeers age, love, and die, and the era of swashbuckling ends. The volume suits readers ready to follow Dumas past adventure into the melancholy close of his great sequence.
30197-farthest-north-vol-i-being-the-rec:
Fridtjof Nansen records the voyage of the ship Fram from 1893 to 1896, with a fifteen months' sleigh journey by Nansen and Lieutenant Johansen, in volume 1 of Farthest North. Harper and Brothers published the New York and London volume in 1897, with an appendix by Otto Sverdrup, captain of the Fram. About one hundred and twenty full-page pictures and many text pictures support the narrative, plus sixteen colored plates from Nansen's own sketches.

Chapters cover introduction, preparations and equipment, the start, farewell to Norway, and a voyage through the Kara Sea. The winter night, the spring and summer of 1894, and a second autumn in the ice follow. Pictures show the Fram leaving Bergen, drift ice in July 1893, and trial trips with dogs. Nansen dedicates the book to her who christened the ship and had the courage to remain behind.
30350-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume 36 of The Philippine Islands, 1493 to 1898, covers 1649 to 1666. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited and annotated the documents, with a historical introduction by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The series draws on explorations, descriptions, histories, and records of Catholic missions in contemporaneous books and manuscripts, showing political, economic, commercial, and religious conditions from first European contact onward.

Documents of 1649 to 1658 open with royal funeral rites at Manila in 1649. Royal aid for Jesuits asked by the Manila cabildo in 1652 follows, with the condition of the Philippines in 1652 by Magino Sola. Jesuit missions in 1655 follow, with a letter from the archbishop of Manila to Felipe IV in 1656. Jesuit memorials on the Moluccas and the Inquisition, and a protest against the Dominican university, close the set, with a description of the islands from Mexico.
30634-the-naples-riviera:
Herbert M. Vaughan writes The Naples Riviera, first published in London in 1907 by Methuen, with twenty-five illustrations in colour by Maurice Greiffenhagen. Vaughan, author of The Last of the Royal Stuarts, dedicates the book in memory of many pleasant days in the sunny south.

A front illustration shows charcoal carriers at Amalfi, setting the tone for a travel book rich in coast, towns, and history. Thirteen chapters move from an introduction and the Vesuvian shore to the dead city, Vesuvius, and the Corniche road. Amalfi, Ravello, Salerno, Paestum, Sorrento, Capri, Ischia, and Puteoli follow, with an index closing the tour.
30776-materials-and-methods-of-fiction-w:
Clayton Hamilton wrote this 1911 guide to writing fiction, with an introduction by Brander Matthews and a dedication to Frederic Taber Cooper. The Chautauqua Press published it, after a 1908 copyright by Baker and Taylor, and Hamilton treats fiction as a craft with rules a writer can learn. His translator's notes show care for spelling and for Stevenson's Master of Ballantrae, among other details.

Eleven chapters move from the purpose of fiction through realism and romance, the nature of narrative, plot, characters, and setting, to point of view and emphasis in narrative. Closing chapters weigh the epic, the drama, and the novel, and the novel, the novelette, and the short story, with the structure of the short story last. It is a clear, early textbook for writers who want to build stories on purpose, not by chance.
31762-the-record-of-currupira:
Robert Abernathy's short story was printed in Fantastic Universe in January 1954. It starts from a striking idea: when Earth reaches Mars, it may find records of prehistoric Earth kept by Martian visitors long ago. Its hero, James Dalton, walks the main exhibit room of New York's Martian Museum as rockets bring home relics from dead Martian cities.

One new exhibit catches his eye, and from ancient Martian records comes the grim song of a creature long forgotten on Earth. Readers get a compact science-fiction tale about archaeology across planets, and about what an alien archive might remember that Earth itself has lost.
31880-physiology-of-the-opera:
Physiology of the Opera, by Scrici and published at Philadelphia in 1852 by Willis P. Hazard, is a satirical dissertation on the opera world of its day. Its introduction refuses an antiquarian parallel matching ancient Greek tragedy against the modern sanguinary Italian opera, comparing Signor Salvi trilling on stage to Thespis jargoning from a dung-cart.

Instead, Scrici holds the mirror up to nature, inviting ladies, young gentlemen with moustaches and gilded lorgnettes, and old papas in stalls to see themselves in the opera house. Readers get a witty mid-nineteenth-century satire of singers, audiences, and the social theatre of opera-going.
31963-the-flying-dutchman-der-fliegende-:
Richard Wagner's romantic opera The Flying Dutchman, in the Metropolitan Opera libretto edition published by Fred Rullman in New York, presents the German libretto with a correct English translation. It is printed speech by speech as on facing pages. The edition calls itself the only correct and authorized edition, with Knabe piano used exclusively.

Its argument introduces the Dutchman, the spectral captain condemned to sail the seas until redeemed by a faithful woman's love. Readers get the full libretto of Wagner's early opera, in German and English, for following the performance or reading the drama at home.
32361-the-prophetic-camera:
John McGreevey's tale, printed in Imagination in August 1953, follows Joey Barrett, a photographer who doubts an old man's claim to photograph the future. Joey swings onto his editor Nugent's desk, heels drumming, and refuses an assignment he calls out of his line. Nugent insists the story is unusual and wants a photographer's view, handing Joey a memo with the address of a man named Jason Ewing.

Joey calls Ewing a crackpot and notes that no brainy reporter will touch the job. Yet the future in Ewing's pictures begins to happen, turning Joey's scorn into alarm. McGreevey builds a compact story about proof, pride, and what a camera can show when its pictures run ahead of events.
32487-a-gift-for-terra:
Fox B. Holden's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in September 1954, opens with Johnny Love alive after a crash landing, head aching, fighting to stay alive. His helmet should have cracked when the landing wrenched acceleration hammocks from their sockets and heaved his suited body across a buckled conning deck, yet it held. Ferris, his companion, was less lucky: his helmet smashed into a million pieces, and Ferris was dead.

Sand sifts in a cold, red river through a rent in the ship's side, trying to bury Johnny before he can stand on a tilted deck. Good Martian Samaritans, the tale's framing note explains, rescued Johnny and offered him the stars, a gift horse others looked into more closely and found an answer to life within. Holden builds a story of rescue, gratitude, and suspicion on an alien world.
32882-lady-cassandra:
Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's novel follows Cassandra Raynor, a wealthy young woman who has everything a grand house and a wide estate can offer, and finds it all dull. Surrounded by old furniture, obedient servants, and a landscape she knows by heart, she longs for a smaller, plainer life that she could shape herself. Her restlessness sets the story in motion, as comfort turns out to be a poor guard against boredom.

The novel then tests Cassandra against marriage, social duty, and the claims of other people. Vaizey writes with a light, observant touch, letting drawing-room talk and small choices carry the weight of larger questions about what a woman of means should want. It is a domestic comedy with a sharp edge, and Cassandra's search for a life that feels her own gives it its drive.
3329-caesar-and-cleopatra:
George Bernard Shaw sets this five-act play on an October night on Egypt's Syrian border. The year is 706 by Roman computation, reckoned afterward as 48 BC, near the end of the thirty-third dynasty. A great radiance of silver fire, the dawn of a moonlit night, rises in the east, under stars and a cloudless sky. Notes to the play follow the five acts.

Caesar, landing in Egypt, meets a girl queen who is still a child in years and already a politician by instinct. Shaw turns history into comedy of education: the Roman teaches Cleopatra statecraft, and she teaches him charm. Caesar the teacher and Cleopatra the pupil reverse their famous roles, and both learn something.
33545-food-of-the-crow-corvus-brachyrhyn:
Dwight Platt's Food of the Crow, Corvus brachyrhynchos Brehm, in South-Central Kansas, published in June 1956, studies what crows eat on the prairie. Issued as volume eight, number eight of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History publications, from pages 477 to 498, the paper sets out stomach contents and seasonal diets. It has four tables. Platt writes with a field naturalist's care.

The paper suits readers of ornithology, offering a short, factual account of crow diet in one region. Its tone is precise and measured, with tables to back its findings. For bird researchers, it is a useful, if narrow, source on a common bird's role in farm country, as pest, scavenger, and neighbor.
33698-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Borgia, Lucrezia to Bradford, John, as volume four, slice three. Its articles include Borglum, Boric acid, boring, Boris Godunov, Borneo, Bornholm, Borodino, boron, borough, Bournemouth, Boulogne, Boulton, bounty, Bourbaki, Bourbon, Bourgeois, Bourges, and Bourget, among many others. Each entry carries the scholarship of the great eleventh edition.

Readers will find compact treatments of history, science, geography, biography, and the arts, from a Russian tsar and a composer to a chemical element and a system of local government. The slice shows the Britannica's ambition to map all knowledge in alphabetical order, with authority and detail. It remains useful for period facts and for tracing how a century ago understood its own world.
3460-old-fritz-and-the-new-era:
Louise Muhlbach writes about Frederick the Great in his old age in this historical novel, translated from the German by Peter Langley. The first book, called Old Fritz, shows the lonely king, his drive to Berlin, his oath of fidelity, and his court, including the singer Wilhelmine Enke. The second book turns to Rosicrucians, Jesuits, and powerful men around the throne.

Goethe appears in Berlin, and German literature itself becomes part of the plot, as the king meets the new era that will outlive him. Muhlbach blends real figures with invented scenes, as popular historical novelists of her time did. The novel gives a lively, if romantic, view of Prussia at the end of Frederick's reign.
3790-major-barbara:
Bernard Shaw sets this comedy in the house of Lady Britomart Undershaft, a managing matron of the upper class who treats the universe as one large house in Wilton Crescent. Her daughter Barbara, a major in the Salvation Army, preaches salvation to the poor, while her father Andrew Undershaft, an arms maker, offers his fortune to save souls by feeding bodies first. The clash between gospel and guns drives the play.

Bill Walker, a rough customer who doubts he has a soul, tests Barbara's faith in a famous scene, while the scholar Cusins watches with Greek parallels in mind. Shaw lets both sides argue well, and the comedy stings precisely because neither side is a fool. Readers who like plays of ideas will find Major Barbara Shaw at his most provocative and most funny.
4978-the-march-of-portola-and-the-discov:
Zoeth S. Eldredge's March of Portola gathers the documents of the expedition that discovered the Bay of San Francisco. An introduction and the march narrative are followed by data on Portola after California, the viceroy's letter to Arriaga, and the causes that led to the San Carlos expedition.

Logs of the San Carlos, the commander's report, and descriptions of the march itself let readers follow the overland party step by step. The volume opens with verse to the city at the Western Gate, warder of two continents. Readers get California's founding journey in its own records, edited for those who want sources, not just story.
5802-a-sketch-of-the-causes-operations-a:
Stephen Palfrey Webb sketches the causes, operations, and results of the San Francisco Vigilance Committee in 1856. Webb, born in Salem in 1804, graduated from Harvard in 1824, studied law, and wrote his sketch in 1874, looking back on a city's crisis. His account traces why citizens formed a vigilance committee, how it acted, and what followed for San Francisco law and order.

It offers a contemporary history of frontier justice, written by a lawyer who knew its legal stakes. Webb weighs the committee's claims against the dangers of mob rule, offering a measured, firsthand perspective. The book suits readers of California history, Gold Rush San Francisco, and debates about law, order, and citizen action in a young city.
6077-history-of-the-donner-party-a-trage:
C. F. McGlashan tells the Donner Party tragedy in the Sierra, dedicating the book to Elizabeth Keiser, one of California's pioneer mothers. His preface pictures the delirium before death by starvation, full of strange fantasies, visions of plenty, comfort, and elegance flitting before dimming eyes.

In the final twilight, a dying man at Donner Lake might rise from his snowy couch and point upward. He describes a beautiful house of walnut inlaid with laurel and ebony, rich with silver, cushions, tapestries, and mirrors. McGlashan writes with pity for pioneers caught by snow, hunger, and dreams of home.
6443-the-wagner-story-book-firelight-tal:
William Henry Frost tells Wagner's music dramas as firelight tales for a girl who seeks him out when he is not over busy to ask for a story. She likes his stories, flattering his vanity, and he likes nothing better than telling them. The contents run from stolen treasure and daughter of the god to hero who knew no fear and end of the Ring. Then come knight of the swan, prize of a song, and blood red sail.

Love potion, minstrel knight, king of the Grail, and ashes complete the set, with pictures of gold shining and beautiful and sunlight following a hero into a cave. By the fire, the little girl takes a stool, lays her cheek on his hand, and looks into flames with him. Frost writes opera plots as hearth tales, where gods, heroes, and cursed gold become stories a child can follow by firelight.
6594-schwatka-s-search-sledging-in-the-a:
William Gilder, second in command, tells how Lieutenant Schwatka sledged through the Arctic in search of the lost Franklin expedition. By 1880, Schwatka had traced the last lost ship to its grave, cleared a harmless people of a foul charge, and brought one body home for burial in kinder soil. A leading English paper hailed the feat in warm terms.

The tale that follows is one of ice, hunger, dogs, and long marches, told by a man who shared the hardship. Gilder writes with the plain pride of a comrade, not with cold science. Schwatka's Search is a stirring true story of Arctic grit and of a mystery at last laid to rest.
6731-the-duenna-a-comic-opera:
Richard Brinsley Sheridan's comic opera The Duenna, first acted at Covent Garden in November 1775, is set in Seville. Lopez enters with a dark lantern past three in the morning, grumbling that to serve a young lover is the hardest service of all. He is no enemy to love, he says, but his master keeps him strolling like a bravo through the streets.

Don Ferdinand, Don Jerome, Don Antonio, Donna Louisa, Donna Clara, and the Duenna herself drive a plot of lovers, friars, and disguise. Sheridan's songs and talk keep the farce bright. The Duenna is a gay, classic comic opera text, full of Spanish color and English wit.
6913-voyages-of-peter-esprit-radisson-be:
Peter Esprit Radisson's own account of his travels among the North American Indians runs from 1652 to 1684. Transcribed from original manuscripts in the Bodleian Library and the British Museum, the narratives come with historical notes and an introduction by Gideon Scull for the Prince Society. The preface stresses that Radisson wrote as a principal actor, with no thought of print.

That plain, unstudied quality is what makes the record trustworthy, after more than two hundred years in manuscript. The voyages trace trade, captivity, council, and travel across the lakes and rivers of the north. Readers meet a French adventurer whose life crossed empires, peoples, and a continent still taking shape.
6988-history-of-the-ottawa-and-chippewa-:
Andrew Blackbird, late United States interpreter at Harbor Springs, Michigan, writes the history of the Ottawa and Chippewa Indians of Michigan, with a grammar of their language and his own family history. The introduction presents him as an educated Indian, son of an Ottawa chief, whose Indian name Mack aw de be nessy means Black Hawk. He took the name Blackbird from the French for black bird, married an educated English woman, and raised four children.

Brought up without schooling in boyhood, he set out blindly for learning with only his brains and his hands. Loyal to the government during the rebellion, he stands as a friend of white people and his own people alike. The book joins tribal history, language lessons, and a personal life into one plain record.
7783-birch-bark-legends-of-niagara:
Birch Bark Legends of Niagara, by Owahyah, retells traditions among the Iroquois, or Six Nations. The tales come from Joinstaga, to whose memory the book is dedicated. Its central story tells of the lunar bow that lights the falls by moonlight, and of the origin of the Wolf totem.

A preface quotes Governor Clinton on the Iroquois confederacy as a remarkable piece of lawmaking. Clinton also notes the injustice done to Native peoples, whose kindness, honor, hospitality, love of truth, and unbroken faith deserve as much telling as their cruelties. Washington Irving is quoted too.
7951-glimpses-of-bengal-selected-from-th:
Sir Rabindranath Tagore's letters from 1885 to 1895 are gathered here in selection, covering what he calls the most productive period of his literary life. Writing when he was young and less known, with leisure and feeling to spare, he sent friends letters full of observation about Bengal. Its rivers and villages, its people, and the thoughts that later fed his poems and stories. The selection reached him years later from the friends who had kept them.

The charm of the book is its informality, since letters written for one reader can be freer than work meant for print. Readers meet Tagore before fame, watching the countryside and turning over ideas. It is an inviting way into his world, and a reminder that some of his finest writing began as private correspondence.
8015-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
In the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, a proclamation allowed the exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the house of God. Ezra tells what followed: the first return under Zerubbabel, the laying of the temple foundations, opposition that halted the work, and its completion under Darius. Ezra himself arrives later, a priest and scribe, to teach the law and reform the community.

The book is short but pivotal, marking the moment Israel became a temple community under Persian rule rather than a kingdom. Its lists of returning families and its letters from Persian kings give it a documentary feel. In the King James Version, Ezra shows a people rebuilding not only walls but identity, around Scripture and worship.
8242-the-world-english-bible-web-ezra:
Ezra, in the World English Bible, opens in the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, when Yahweh stirs the king's spirit so that he proclaims throughout his kingdom. In writing, that the God of heaven has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem. Whoever among the people wishes may go up to Judah and build the house of Yahweh, the God of Israel. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows the return, the temple's rebuilding, and Ezra's reforms.

The modern wording keeps the Persian decrees and family lists clear, so the story of restoration reads steadily. Ezra shows a community remade around worship and law after exile. For readers who want the post-exilic history without archaic phrasing, this version gives the account plainly and completely.
8938-zenobia-or-the-fall-of-palmyra:
William Ware writes Zenobia, or the Fall of Palmyra. Letters from Piso, a Roman lately dwelling on the Coelian hill, now writing from the great city of the East. He struggles to believe it is really he who sits and writes. Different are nature and works of man from the West, that at times he seems subject to a dream. Rousing himself, he finds he is awake, basking in Palmyra's warm skies, amid splendour and luxury. Yet longing to be in Rome again beside his friend Curtius, discoursing as they used to do.

Through Piso's letters, Ware tells the rise and fall of Queen Zenobia, who challenged Rome and lost her desert empire. The epistolary form lets a Roman observer admire Palmyra while judging its queen. Ware's novel, a staple of American classical fiction, blends history, romance, and moral reflection.
9254-biographical-stories-from-true-stor:
Hawthorne wrote these biographical stories for children, from True Stories of History and Biography. Contents include Benjamin West, Isaac Newton, Samuel Johnson, Oliver Cromwell, Benjamin Franklin, and Queen Christina. Hawthorne states his care plainly: children are sacred, and he would not cast anything into a young heart that might embitter its waters.

Each life is told as a story with a moral, meant to form character as well as knowledge. The book remains a classic of children's biography, earnest, clear, and shaped by Hawthorne's sense of responsibility to the young.
9995-little-journey-to-puerto-rico-for-i:
Marian M. George wrote this school book in the Plan Book series to answer children's questions about America's new possessions. Why were men in streets and shops talking of them, and why were newspapers and lawmakers full of the subject? The book begins with those very questions.

It then leads young readers to Puerto Rico, lately come into the possession of the United States, with Hawaii and other islands named beside it. The tone is simple and direct, for intermediate and upper grades. Pupils get geography, history, and citizenship lessons woven into one short journey.
a-first-family-of-tasajara:
Bret Harte opens in the general store of Sidon settlement in Contra Costa, where a gust of wind shakes the wooden building and sets the straw hats swinging on their beam. Four loafers sit out the weather while talk turns to the great family of the place. Tasajara's first family rose with California itself, from camp beginnings to ranch wealth.

The novel follows that family's pride, marriages, and slow decline as the old order of Spanish grants and mining money gives way to new men. Harte writes social comedy with a Western setting: balls, lawsuits, and duels of manners among people who remember when the land was wilderness. His irony is kind and his eye for pretension exact.
a-sketch-of-the-causes-operations-and-re:
A Sketch of the Causes, Operations and Results of the San Francisco Vigilance Committee in 1856, by Stephen Palfrey Webb, gives a mayor's eyewitness account of America's most famous vigilante movement. Webb, a Harvard graduate and Salem lawyer who served as mayor of Salem, went west about 1853 and was mayor of San Francisco in 1854 and 1855. He watched the riotous mobs that followed the Gold Rush at close range.

After returning east, Webb lectured on what he had seen and expanded his notes into this sketch, dated 1874. The Committee of 1856, formed after shootings shook the city, enrolled thousands, seized accused men from jail, tried them, and hanged several, defying the state government in the name of order. Webb's paper, preserved by his family, is valued as firsthand testimony from a trained observer who stood on the ground, neither rioter nor committee man.
a-vanished-arcadia-being-some-account-of:
R. B. Cunninghame Graham recounts the Jesuit missions of Paraguay from 1607 to 1767, as his title page states. Jesuit priests gathered the Guaraní people into mission towns, called reductions, deep in South America. There they built churches, taught crafts and music, and shielded the Guaraní from slave raiders and harsh settlers.

His chapters move from Sebastian Cabot and the first expeditions through Father Montoya's great retreat down the Paraná, quarrels with bishops and governors, and the final expulsion of the Jesuits. Graham writes with sympathy for the lost mission world and with a traveler's feel for the land. The map and the records behind the text give it weight.
antony-and-cleopatra:
William Shakespeare's tragedy, in the old-spelling text of this edition, ranges between Alexandria and Rome as two worlds pull at Mark Antony. Antony, one of Rome's three rulers, lingers in Egypt with Queen Cleopatra while affairs at home decay. His wife dies, a rival grows stronger, and duty calls him back too late.

The play moves through councils, feasts, and battles on land and sea, ending at Actium and in Egypt again. Antony and Cleopatra choose love and pride over safety, and both meet grand, theatrical deaths. Shakespeare gives Cleopatra wit, rage, and splendor, and gives Rome cold ambition in young Octavius Caesar.
biographical-stories-from-true-stories-o:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote these biographical stories for children as part of True Stories of History and Biography. His preface takes the duty solemnly: the author regards children as sacred, and would not cast anything into a young heart's fountain that might embitter it. Six lives make the set — Benjamin West, Sir Isaac Newton, Samuel Johnson, Oliver Cromwell, Benjamin Franklin, and Queen Christina.

Boyhood scenes carry the lessons. Young Oliver Cromwell, called Noll, is presented at court after a few questions in Latin grammar. The little prince extends his hand, grave and dignified, not to shake but to be kissed. Noll thrusts it aside with a rude laugh: I owe him no duty — why should I kiss it? Hawthorne lets the future Lord Protector announce himself in one gesture, history told as childhood anecdote for the fireside.
birch-bark-legends-of-niagara:
Owahyah gathered these birch bark legends of Niagara from traditions among the Iroquois, or Six Nations. He dedicates the book to the memory of Joinstaga. From that chief he obtained many legends of the almost forgotten past. Its centrepiece is a story of the lunar-bow, the rainbow that adorns the Falls by moonlight, told as the origin of the wolf totem.

Council scenes frame the tales. Chiefs smoke while Black Snake takes up his bow and arrow again. He calls for young braves to track the deer and carry the meat back. A feast and dance follow each council, as the sun sinks beyond Lake Ontario. Owahyah writes in the romantic manner of the period, preserving Six Nations tradition through a settler's dated lens.
britannica-1911-abbot-ezra:
Ezra Abbot receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbot, an American Bible scholar born in Maine in 1819, graduated at Bowdoin in 1840 and came to Cambridge at Andrews Norton's call. Harvard made him assistant librarian, then Bussey professor of New Testament study.

His card catalogue at Harvard set a model, part dictionary and part system. A list of 5,300 writings on the future life shows his range as a bibliographer. Four hundred articles went into Smith's Dictionary of the Bible, enlarged with Hackett. Service on the American revision committee and help to Gregory's Greek Testament work followed. His Authorship of the Fourth Gospel holds the chief place among his books. He died at Cambridge in 1884.
britannica-1911-abenezra:
Abraham ben Meir Ibn Ezra, called Abenezra, receives a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed by William Bacher. Ibn Ezra, born at Toledo in 1092 or 1093, left Spain before 1140 and wandered North Africa, Egypt, Italy, France, and England till death. Hebrew letters owe him a founding debt.

Grammar came first: Moznayim and Zahot opened Hebrew grammar in Hebrew, on Hayyuj's system, which he also translated. Bible commentaries made his fame, above all on the Pentateuch, hunting the plain sense on firm grammar. Wit and sharp turns mark his prose. Spinoza later used his hints toward Pentateuch criticism. Neo-platonic thought and astrology color his religious philosophy. He died in January 1167, place unknown.
britannica-1911-abracadabra:
Abracadabra receives an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The word, akin to Abraxas, served the Basilidian Gnostics as a magic formula calling kind spirits against disease and ill luck. Abraxas stones worn as amulets carry it still.

Serenus Sammonicus, a Gnostic physician, set the ritual: the word written, folded crosswise, hung by linen at the pit of the stomach for nine days. Before sunrise on the last day it went, cast backward, into an east-running stream. Letters shrink line by line into a triangle in the usual layout. Later ages spread the charm, then turned the word to scorn for any glib cure-all claim.
britannica-1911-abraham-a-sancta-clara:
Abraham a Sancta Clara receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abraham, born Ulrich Megerle at Kreenheinstetten in 1644, joined the Barefooted Augustinians in 1662 and rose to prior provincial of his order. Vienna made him court preacher in 1669.

Crowds flocked to hear him. Homely force of language, grotesque humour, and even-handed severity against the follies of every class, the court included, fill the entry's portrait. A man of the people in the pulpit, he could also rise to loftier, dignified thought. His didactic novel Judas der Erzschelm stands as the best sample of his style in print. He died at Vienna in 1709, his works often reprinted, if with spurious additions.
britannica-1911-accra:
Accra is a port on the Gulf of Guinea and, since 1876, capital of the British Gold Coast colony, with about twenty thousand people. The town grew up around three forts built close together: British St James, Dutch Crevecoeur, and Danish Christiansborg, the last two passing to Britain in 1850 and 1871. Their names survive in the town's three quarters, James Town, Ussher Town, and Christiansborg.

No harbour serves the port, so steamers anchor a mile out and surf boats land goods and passengers. After a great fire in 1894, more substantial buildings replaced mud hovels. Christiansborg fort houses the governor, and Accra governs itself through a town council of nominated and elected members.
britannica-1911-agora:
Agora was originally the Greek people's assembly. Kings or nobles convoked it in primitive times. Nobles alone held rights of speech and vote. The people expressed opinion by applause or disapproval. The word then transferred to the assembly's place. Convenience as a meeting-place changed its use further. The agora became the general resort of Greek cities. Public and commercial intercourse centred there. Rome's forum corresponds to it generally.

Daily life filled the classical agora. Nearly all public traffic was conducted there. Forenoons were its busiest hours, men only attending. Slaves did most of the purchasing for households. Foreigners and metics paid a toll for market rights. Citizens traded free of that charge. Festivals also used the open area. Cimon planted trees in Athens's agora.
britannica-1911-agra:
Agra is an ancient city of India. A district and division bear its name. The city stands in the United Provinces. It holds the most perfect specimens of Mogul architecture. Position gave Agra importance in all eras. The river Jumna washes its fort's walls. That river was Bengal delta traffic's natural highway. It also formed a frontier defence line. Aryan settlers of the Ganges plain held it. Western freebooters pressed from the Central Indian highlands.

Empire builders made it a capital. Sikandar Lodi moved his court there about 1500. Baber captured the city in 1526. The Koh-i-noor diamond was part of his loot. Akbar built the present great fort of red sandstone. The Taj Mahal's inlaid marble crowns the city's fame.
britannica-1911-alcantara:
Alcantara, a small seaport of Brazil, is noticed briefly in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the state of Maranhao, on the western shore of the bay of Sao Marcos. By water it lies sixteen miles from the city of Maranhao, the state capital across the bay. The entry is one of the shortest in its stretch of the alphabet.

What the notice does record is a working port and its hinterland. Alcantara has a fairly good harbour, a point of real weight on that coast. Excellent cotton and rice are grown in the country around the town. Both crops are shipped out through the harbour, which is the town's reason for being. The entry's brevity matches the place: a small shipping point for two prized farm products, fixed by its bay, its distance, and its trade.
britannica-1911-alcira:
Walls ring Alcira, a town of eastern Spain in Valencia province, and rich wet ground rings the walls. Groves of palm, orange, and mulberry crowd close, with low rice swamps beyond that leave the area somewhat unwholesome. The town stands on the left bank of the Jucar, on the rail line from Valencia to Alicante, and counted 20,572 people in 1900.

Silk, fruit, and rice head its goods, all drawn from that damp, fertile soil. Some link Alcira to the Roman place Saetabicula, though the tie is offered with care. Under Moorish rule in the middle ages it thrived as a trading post. Its later life kept the same cast: crops and trade borne by the river plain.
britannica-1911-aldabra:
Aldabra is a ring of islands in the Indian Ocean, an atoll some forty miles round that clasps a shallow lagoon. The group forms part of the British colony of Seychelles and lies 265 miles north-west of the top point of Madagascar. Channels cut the ring into four islands, and small islets dot the lagoon inside.

Grande Terre, or South Island, makes three fifths of the ring. West Island, Polymnie, and Middle Island make the rest. The land spans near sixty square miles in all, and just 127 people lived there in 1906. The isles rise twenty to eighty feet over the sea in rough coral rock and limestone, with scant soil and cliffs that hang over the water. Their wild life leans toward Madagascar and the Comoros: huge tortoises among the creeping beasts, two kinds of bat, and birds and land shells near to Comoro forms.
britannica-1911-almora:
High in the Himalayas, Almora serves as chief town and headquarters for the Kumaon division of the United Provinces in British India. Its ridge-top site stands 5,494 feet above the sea, and 8,596 people lived there in 1901. Schools mark the town: a college named for Sir Henry Ramsay, a government high school, and a Christian girls' school, alongside a large cantonment.

History turned on two captures. Gurkhas seized Almora in 1790 and raised a fort at the ridge's eastern end; in April 1815 a British victory there closed the war with Nepal, bringing Kumaon's annexation. The district around it, formed in 1891, spans 5,419 square miles of mountains between the upper Ganges and the Kali, grows tea, and holds the military sanatorium of Ranikhet.
britannica-1911-alompra-aloung-p-houra:
Alompra, or Aloung P'houra (1711–1760), was the founder of the last Burmese dynasty. Born at Mōtshobo, a small village north-west of Ava, he was of humble origin and had risen to be chief of his native village. When the king of Pegu invaded Burma in 1752 and the country's chiefs submitted, Alompra refused, regained his village, and defeated the Peguan troops sent against him.

A thousand Burmese rallied to him, and Ava was recovered before the end of 1753. He founded Rangoon in 1755 and conquered Pegu by 1757, then crushed a Peguan revolt. The entry weighs his suspected approval of the massacre of the English at Negrais in 1759, and records his death on 15 May 1760 while invading Siam. It credits him with military genius, political sagacity, and efforts to improve the administration of justice.
britannica-1911-angelico-fra:
Fra Angelico (1387–1455) was an Italian painter, born Guido at Vicchio in the Tuscan province of Mugello. Giovanni was his name in religion, taken when he entered the Dominican order at Fiesole in 1408 after a year as a novice. The name Angelico, meaning the angelic, was a term of praise attached to him early, and he was later beatified by the church.

Beyond all other painters of his century, Fra Angelico represents pietistic painting, art in service of devotion. The entry traces his training, with Lorenzo Monaco and the Sienese school shaping his style, and surveys his works from the Florentine Certosa commissions onward. His pictured visions of the divine persons, the hierarchy of heaven, and the glory of the redeemed receive special attention. A long list of modern books about the painter closes the long, admiring account.
britannica-1911-angora:
Angora, or Enguri, is a city of Turkey in Asia, the ancient Ancyra. It is capital of the vilayet of the same name. It stands on a steep hill rising five hundred feet above the plain, on the left bank of a tributary of the Sakaria. Constantinople lies about 220 miles west-north-west. The ruined citadel crowns the hill. The town below is poorly built, with narrow streets and houses of sun-dried mud brick.

Fine remains survive from Greek, Roman, and Byzantine times. The temple of Rome and Augustus is the most remarkable. Its walls carry the famous Monumentum Ancyranum. Ancyra was the centre of the Tectosages, a Gaulish tribe in Galatia. It became capital of the Roman province in 25 B.C. Persians, Arabs, Seljuk Turks, and Crusaders held it in turn. The Ottoman Turks took it in 1360. A great battle near the city in 1402 opens the closing history.
britannica-1911-angra:
Angra, or Angra do Heroismo, is a town in the Portuguese Azores. Its name means Bay of Heroism. That name dates from 1829. It honours the town's defence against the Miguelist party. Angra was once capital of the whole archipelago. It now heads a district covering three islands. Those islands are Terceira, St George, and Graciosa. The town itself stands on Terceira's south coast.

The population in 1900 was 10,788. Angra hosts a military command and a Catholic bishop. Its chief buildings are the cathedral and military college. An arsenal and an observatory also stand there. The harbour was once a celebrated naval station. It now holds little commercial or strategic importance. Fruit, especially pineapples, forms the main export trade. Queen Maria II sheltered at Angra from 1830 to 1833.
britannica-1911-aymara:
Aymara, anciently Colla, are a South American Indian people who once held the country around Lake Titicaca and the Andean valleys nearby. They now form the chief native element in Bolivia, though of very mixed blood, numbering about half a million with half-breeds counted.

Their Titicaca homeland was holy ground even to the Incas, whose legends traced all their civilization to that region. Before Inca conquest in the 13th and 14th centuries, the Aymara had built a high culture, witnessed by the great stone ruins of Tiahuanaco. Under Inca rule they kept their own language and certain privileges, a sign, the entry suggests, that their conquerors believed themselves of Aymara blood. A short, thick-set build and great chest mark the pure type described.
britannica-1911-bamra:
Bamra was a feudatory state of India, in the province of Bengal. It covered 1,988 square miles and held 123,378 people in 1901. Its estimated revenue was £5,000, and it paid a tribute of £100. The capital was Deogarh.

Most of the country is forest, yielding only timber and lac, though it is said to be rich in iron ore. The Bengal-Nagpur railway touches its northern border, with a station at Bamra town. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that Bamra was one of five Uriya feudatory states moved from the Central Provinces to Bengal when that province was reshaped in October 1905. The entry is short and keeps to these bare facts.
britannica-1911-barra:
Barra, or Barray, is an island of the Outer Hebrides in Inverness-shire, Scotland, lying about five miles south-west of South Uist. It is eight miles long and from two to four miles broad, though at one sandy isthmus it narrows to a few hundred yards. Its population in 1901 was 2,362, and its rock is gneiss.

Heaval, its highest hill, rises 1,260 feet, and small lochs dot the island. The chief village is Castlebay, where the Glasgow steamer calls once a week, named for Kishmul Castle, stronghold of the MacNeills of Barra, an old Highland clan. The 1911 Britannica entry notes ancient chapels, Danish duns, and Druidical circles, and praises the cod, ling, and herring fisheries and the island's famous cockles.
britannica-1911-bartolommeo-di-pagholo-f:
Fra Bartolommeo di Pagholo (1475–1517), an Italian painter of history and portraits born near Florence, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is also called Baccio della Porta, from his home near the Porta Romana. Trained by Cosimo Roselli, he studied Leonardo's works, and his early fresco of the Last Judgment, painted with Mariotto Albertinelli, showed his grace and skill. Work for a Dominican convent brought him under Savonarola's strong influence.

Grief changed his path. Shaken by Savonarola's cruel death, Bartolommeo entered the convent himself and gave up painting for some years, resuming only at his superior's command. Friendship with Raphael followed: he learned perspective from the younger man, while Raphael gained in colour and drapery from him. Most of his works are altar-pieces. His St Mark is named as his masterpiece, and his St Sebastian was so moving that it had to be removed from display.
britannica-1911-barton-clara:
Clara Barton (1821– ), an American philanthropist born in Oxford, Massachusetts, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. She began teaching at sixteen, but ill health ended that work, and from 1854 to 1857 she clerked in the Patent Office at Washington. During the Civil War she distributed large amounts of supplies to wounded soldiers. Afterwards she ran a records bureau in Washington that searched for missing men and marked more than twelve thousand graves at Andersonville.

Europe turned Barton toward the Red Cross. In Switzerland in 1869 the International Committee sought her help, and she worked with the society in the Franco-Prussian War, earning the Iron Cross. Back home she campaigned until the United States joined the Geneva treaty and founded the American Red Cross, which she led as first president until 1904. Her American amendment extended Red Cross relief to famines, floods, and other disasters in peacetime.
britannica-1911-berbera:
Berbera is the chief town and main port of the British Somaliland protectorate in North-East Africa, 155 miles south of Aden. It stands at the head of a deep inlet, the only fully sheltered haven on the south side of the Gulf of Aden. The protectorate’s commissioner lives there, and the Somaliland battalion has its headquarters in the town.

Two piers, warehouses and eleven to thirteen fathoms of water at the entrance serve ocean steamers well. The town splits in two: the native town east, the new town west, laid out by the Egyptians in 1875–1877. Fewer than ten thousand people live there for good, but the trading season from October to April swells the crowd past thirty thousand.
britannica-1911-bora:
Bora is the Italian name for a violent cold wind from the north and north-east that strikes the Adriatic, above all the Istrian and Dalmatian coasts. The entry explains the cause in plain physical terms. In winter the air over the northern Mediterranean shores already tends to slide downhill from the cold mountains to the warmer sea.

When a storm centre forms over the Mediterranean, the winds in its north-western quarter pull that cold northern air down hard, and during the storm's passage the bora blows. The same wind is found at Novorossiysk on the Black Sea. In character it is exactly like the mistral of Provence and the French Mediterranean coast, the entry says, and the short account ends on that comparison.
britannica-1911-caprera:
Caprera is an island off the north-east coast of Sardinia. It is about a mile in length. A bridge joins it to the island of La Maddalena. This very short 1911 Britannica entry gives its one great claim to fame. The island is known for its link with Garibaldi. He first settled there in 1854. He made the island his home from that year.

Garibaldi died on Caprera on 2 June 1882. His tomb stands on the island still. Italians from all parts visit it each year. They come on the anniversary of his death.
