The entry adds one older note to the Garibaldi story. Roman remains have been found on the island. A bust of Maximian was among the finds. The whole notice is only a few lines long. It gives the size, the bridge, the tomb and the Roman finds.
britannica-1911-capybara:
The capybara is the largest living rodent in the world. It is also called the carpincho. This 1911 Britannica article describes the animal. Its limbs are moderately long, with partly webbed toes. There are four toes in front and three behind. The nails resemble small hooves. Its hair is sparse, its ears short, and it has no tail. Its last molar is huge.

Capybaras are water rodents of South America. They haunt the banks of lakes and rivers. Some live where the water is brackish. They move in herds along the banks. Most of the day they rest in cover. They feed in the evening and in the morning. When disturbed, they take to the water at once. They swim and dive with real skill, staying under water for minutes at a time. Their food is water-plants, bark, and farm crops.
britannica-1911-carnivora:
Carnivora is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the zoological order that takes in lions, tigers, and wolves, along with bears, smaller flesh-eaters, and the seals and their kin. The entry defines the group by shared structure rather than by diet alone, since some members eat largely vegetable food. It sets the order apart from the extinct Creodonta and then lays out the marks that its members hold in common.

The entry details teeth, jaws, and senses in depth. Members are clawed mammals with at least four toes on each foot, small pointed incisors, and strong curved canine teeth. The lower jaw hinges in a deep socket, the stomach stays simple, and the brain always bears folds. Further sections work through the skeleton and soft organs, trait by trait. Readers get a full anatomical portrait of the order as science then understood it.
britannica-1911-carora:
Carora is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an inland town in the state of Lara, Venezuela. The town stands on the Carora river, a branch of the Tocuyo, about 54 miles west by south of Barquisimeto and 1128 feet above sea level. Its population was estimated at 6000 in 1908. The entry calls it comparatively well built, with a fine parish church, a Franciscan convent, and a hermitage.

Carora was founded in 1754, and its colonial years brought real prosperity, when its people numbered 9000 to 10,000. The surrounding country is given mainly to raising horses, mules, and cattle. Alongside hides and leather, the town exports rubber and other forest products. The short entry thus pairs a smaller present with a richer colonial past. Readers get the town's setting, its church buildings, and the farm trade that sustained it at the time of writing.
britannica-1911-chatterji-bankim-chandra:
Bankim Chandra Chatterji (1838–1894) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Indian novelist born in the Twenty four Parganas in Bengal. He was a Brahman by caste. He studied at Hugli College and at the Presidency College in Calcutta. He was the first man to take the B.A. degree at Calcutta University, in 1858. He entered the Indian civil service and served as deputy magistrate across Bengal. He retired in 1891 with honours.

The entry calls him beyond question the greatest novelist of India in the nineteenth century. Sir Walter Scott and the European romance writers shaped his schooling. On that model he created a school of fiction in India. His first historical novel, Durges Nandini, modelled on Scott, caused a sensation in Bengal. Social novels followed from 1872, starting with the Poison Tree. For over twenty years the educated public of Bengal read his novels eagerly.
britannica-1911-chimaera:
Chimaera, in Greek mythology, was a fire-breathing female monster, like a lion in the fore part, a goat in the middle and a dragon behind. Homer's Iliad, as cited here, gives her three heads matching those three forms. She devastated Caria and Lycia for a time, the entry says. Bellerophon finally slew her, ending the ravages in those lands of Asia Minor.

The myth may rise from the volcanic nature of the soil of Lycia, a view the entry takes from Pliny and Servius. Works found there show the Chimaera in the simple form of a lion alone. In modern art she is usually shown as a lion with a goat's head in the middle of the back, as in the bronze Chimaera of Arezzo. The word now serves in general speech for any fantastic idea or fiction of the imagination.
britannica-1911-ciudad-de-cura:
Ciudad de Cura is an inland town of the state of Aragua, Venezuela, 55 miles south-west of Carácas, near the Lago de Valencia. Its people numbered 12,198 in 1891, and it stands 1,598 feet above sea level in a broad, fertile valley. Streams there run southward to the Guárico river and northward to the lake, dividing at the town's watershed. Traffic between Puerto Cabello and the Guárico plains has passed through it since early colonial times.

That through traffic made the town an important commercial centre with a high reputation for enterprise in Venezuela. Hides, cheese, coffee, cacao and beans are sent down from it to the coast for export. Ciudad de Cura was founded in 1730, the entry records at its close. It suffered severely in the war of independence, a loss set against its colonial trade role in the short account given.
britannica-1911-cleopatra:
Cleopatra was the regular name of queens of Egypt in the Ptolemaic dynasty, but the best known was the daughter of Ptolemy XIII Auletes, born in 69 or 68 B.C. At seventeen she became queen jointly with her younger brother Ptolemy Dionysus, whose wife she was to become by Egyptian custom. Deprived of authority a few years later, she withdrew into Syria to prepare recovery by arms. Julius Caesar then followed Pompey into Egypt and took up her cause.

Caesar's war cost Ptolemy his life and restored her, and she lived openly with Caesar in Rome until his assassination drove her home. She then became ally and mistress of Mark Antony in the struggle that followed. Octavian declared war and defeated them at Actium in 31 B.C. Antony killed himself in a mistaken belief that she was already dead. Cleopatra ended her life on 29 August 30 B.C.
britannica-1911-clepsydra:
Clepsydra, from Greek words for stealing and water, was the chronometer of the Greeks and Romans, measuring time by the flow of water. In simplest form it was a short-necked earthenware globe, pierced at the bottom with small holes. Water escaped or stole away through those holes at a set rate. Courts used it to limit speeches, giving the phrases aquam dare, to give speaking time, and aquam perdere, to waste time.

Glass clepsydrae served early in place of the sun-dial, though seasonal hours and falling pressure troubled the measure. Keeping the water level uniform remedied the slowing flow as the vessel emptied. Plato is said to have invented a complex clepsydra marking night and day hours. Ctesibius of Alexandria, about 135 B.C., made a hydraulic clock. In it water wheels raised a small figure that pointed out the hours with a stick.
britannica-1911-cobra:
Cobra, Naja tripudians, is a poisonous colubrine snake of the family Elapidae, known also as the hooded snake, cobra di capello or naga. Elongated front ribs can be raised and brought forward to expand the neck at will into a broad disk or hood. That hood gives the snake its common names in several tongues. Maxillary bones bear the fangs, of which only the front one connects with the poison gland at any time.

Replacement fangs lie loose in the flesh behind, moving forward and fixing to the bone when the working fang is destroyed. The poison gland is about the size of an almond, and the snake reaches nearly six feet long. Typical colouring is yellowish to dark brown, with a black and white spectacle mark on the back of the hood. Habits are mainly nocturnal, and it hides under logs and in hut roofs.
britannica-1911-coelentera:
Coelentera names a group or grade of the animal kingdom. Its weight in zoology grew after the first article on it in 1887. The group shrank in one way, though. The sponges were raised to a phylum of their own, the Parazoa. For the rest, Lankester proposed the name Enterocoela in 1900.

Two layers of cells set these animals apart from the Protozoa. No protozoan shows two such layers with split tasks. The entry works through the group's main branches in detail. It contrasts them by plain marks of build. The Hydrozoa lack a gullet and inner partitions. Their outer muscles run lengthwise and their inner muscles run in rings. The account ends with lines of descent toward the Anthozoa, which gave up free swimming as adults.
britannica-1911-coimbra:
Coimbra is the capital of an administrative district in Portugal, once part of the province of Beira. It stands on the north bank of the river Mondego, 115 miles north-east of Lisbon. Its people numbered 18,144 in 1900. The town climbs rising ground and looks fine from across the river. Up close, its streets are narrow and plain.

One thing gives the town its rank. It holds the only university in the kingdom. That school began at Lisbon in 1291 and settled at Coimbra for good in 1527. Five faculties teach more than 1,300 students. The library holds about 150,000 books. Hospitals serve the medical side, and an observatory serves maths. Old churches, a ruined convent and the Quinta das Lagrimas fill the rest. Quakes and French troops mark its later history.
britannica-1911-copra:
Copra is the dried, broken kernel of the coconut, and it is the form in which the coconut crop is shipped for trade. Coconut oil is drawn from it by boiling and pressing.

 The word came into Spanish and Portuguese from a Malay term for the nut, with a Hindustani form beside it. The hosted entry holds that one trade fact and the word's path, and no more. For the palm itself and its growth it points the reader to the entry on the coconut palm. The description therefore stays with the kernel, the oil drawn from it and the name, since the stub gives nothing further to draw on.
britannica-1911-ctenophora:
The Ctenophora are a class of jelly-fish, set apart as Coelentera that show both radial and two-sided symmetry. Huxley briefly treated them in 1875, but their fine structure stayed little known. Chun's monograph of 1880, on the kinds in the Bay of Naples, changed that. Their marks are a gullet, a part-gelatinous inner tissue, and eight meridian rows of swimming paddles. Save in one genus, they lack stinging cells.

A common British kind, Hormiphora, shows the plan plainly. It is an egg-shaped ball of clear jelly, mouth at the pointed pole and a sense organ at the broad pole. Two long feathery tentacles hang down and can be drawn into pouches. The hosted text opens with a figure's labels, then works through canals, gut, and organs in close anatomical detail. A literature list closes the entry.
britannica-1911-culebra:
Culebra is the smaller of two islands in the Virgin Passage, just east of Porto Rico. It lies about eighteen miles from Cape San Juan and rises from the same drowned shelf as the greater Antilles. The island measures three miles by six, and its surface is low and fairly even. Winds sweep it unchecked, so rain falls in a short season only. Its people must store rainwater in cisterns for drinking.

The soil is fertile, and cattle, poultry, vegetables, and small fruits are raised. Culebra has been a dependency of Porto Rico since 1879, and a ward of the Vieques district. In 1902 the American navy chose Playa Sardinas harbour on its south side as a fleet rendezvous. Marine camps followed on shore. That naval use gave the small island an outsized weight, and its population grew from 704 in 1899 to nearly 1,200 in 1903.
britannica-1911-cullera:
Cullera is a seaport of eastern Spain in the province of Valencia, at the mouth of the river Jucar on the Mediterranean. It ends the Valencia to Silla to Cullera railway, and its population in 1900 was 11,947. The town is walled and holds a ruined Moorish citadel, large barracks, churches, convents, and a hospital. Cape Cullera, a marked headland with a lighthouse, closes the hills to the east. A rich farming district, noted for rice, spreads south and west.

Farming and fishing occupy the people, with a coasting trade to other Mediterranean ports besides. In 1903 the harbour took 66 vessels of about 25,000 tons. Grain, rice, and fruit went out, and guano came in. The town of Sueca lies four miles west-north-west by rail. Citadel, cape, rice fields, and harbour traffic make up the entry's whole picture. No history of the town is offered beyond the Moorish ruin it keeps.
britannica-1911-demerara: Demerara is named in the entry as one of the three settlements of British Guiana. It takes its name from the river Demerara, and the entry gives no further detail of its own. For the country itself it simply directs the reader onward: See Guiana. Nothing more is stated here about the settlement, its land, or its people, and the whole entry amounts to that single cross-reference.
c-f-meyer-die-versuchung-des-pescara:
A great general stands tempted to betray his emperor and seize Italy for himself in C. F. Meyer's Die Versuchung des Pescara, given here in German. The Temptation of Pescara sets the Marquis of Pescara at a crisis of the Italian wars, courted by offers of a crown. Meyer turns the moment into a study of ambition resisted.

His prose is precise and lapidary, every sentence cut like stone. Dying of wounds and courted by temptation, Pescara becomes a Renaissance prince in a moral laboratory. Meyer, the Swiss master of the historical novella, works here at his finest. The past feels close enough to touch, and the psychology stays modern. Few novellas pack so much statecraft and soul into so few pages.
caesar-and-cleopatra:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Caesar and Cleopatra, a play in five acts set in Egypt in 48 BC, as Julius Caesar invades during Egypt's civil war. Young Queen Cleopatra hides near the Sphinx, frightened of the Romans. Caesar meets her there and treats her with amused patience. Shaw's Caesar is aging, bald under an oak wreath, and wiser than everyone around him.

Court scenes bring in King Ptolemy, his adviser Pothinus, and Caesar's blunt officer Rufio. Britannus, Caesar's British secretary, supplies comedy with his shocked respectability. Cleopatra learns statecraft, cruelty, and charm under Caesar's eye. Shaw closes the volume with explanatory notes on his characters. Readers get history rewritten as witty argument, where talk matters as much as battles and Caesar teaches a queen how power works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abdera: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abdera names Abdera, now Bouloustra, a titular see of Rhodope province on Thrace's south coast. The place was founded about 656 years before Christ. Nothing further is recorded in the entry, which stands as a bare geographical and historical note identifying the ancient see and its modern name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-a-san:
Abraham a Sancta Clara, a Discalced Augustinian friar, preached and wrote popular devotional books. He was born at Messkirch in Baden in 1644 and died on 1 December 1709. Eighth of nine children of a prosperous serf who kept a tavern, he was baptized John Ulrich. He was schooled in his village and at Messkirch, passed through the Jesuit school at Ingolstadt, and after his father's death was adopted by his uncle, a canon of Altotting.

In 1662 he joined the Discalced Augustinians at Vienna, taking the name Abraham in his uncle's honour, with a Sancta Clara added. Ordained in 1666, he preached at Taxa near Augsburg and was recalled to Vienna. In 1677 he became imperial court preacher to Leopold I and lived through the plague year of 1679. His vivid preaching and devotional books made him a popular voice, and the entry traces his works and their later study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-ben-m:
Abraham ben Meir Aben-Ezra, also called Ibn Ezra, was a famed Spanish rabbi, Toledo-born in 1092. He died on a journey from Rome or Rodez toward home on 23 January 1167. He excelled in philosophy and astronomy, in medicine and poetry, and in linguistics and exegesis. The Wise, the Great, and the Admirable Doctor were his epithets. Driven from Toledo by vexations inflicted on the Jews, he travelled widely through Europe, Egypt, and Palestine.

His chief work, a commentary on the Sacred Books, is nearly complete except for Paralipomenon, with his Pentateuch commentary in several revisions. He held to the literal sense, shunning rabbinic allegory and cabbalistic extravagance, yet stayed faithful to Jewish tradition. His independent criticism struck some writers as near rationalism, while his other books, like the Book of the Secrets of the Law, follow cabbalistic views and reflect his unsettled travelling life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agra:
Agra is an archdiocese in British India, lying between 25 degrees 30 minutes and 32 degrees north latitude and 75 and 81 degrees east longitude. Its area is 91,843 square miles. Its population by the last census is 28,086,364. When missions were first introduced, Mohammedanism was India's predominant religion, while Hinduism was the primitive religion. Most of the population then, as now, followed it.

The Archdiocese of Agra grew out of the Tibet Mission, the first regular establishment in this part of India. Since 1703 the Sacred Congregation of Propaganda assigned the Tibet mission to the Capuchins of the Marca d'Ancona. From 1704 to 1808 some thirty bands of missionaries, of two or three to eleven or twelve men, were sent out. None were sent from 1808 to 1823, owing to Europe's unsettled state. Ludovic Micara, consecrated bishop on 13 April 1820 for the Tibet-Hindustan Mission, was prevented by circumstances from leaving Europe, where he died a cardinal archbishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-rod:
Alexandre Rodrigues Ferreira was a Brazilian naturalist and explorer, born at Bahia in 1756 and dead at Lisbon in 1815. Sent to Portugal for training, he studied at the University of Coimbra. He taught natural history there, and in 1778 was called to Lisbon to work in the Ajuda Museum. For five years he catalogued its specimens and wrote learned monographs and reports, winning election to the Lisbon Academy of Sciences.

The Portuguese government charged Ferreira with a scientific expedition into the interior of Brazil, which he undertook in 1783 and spent nine years on. From Marajó Island he crossed to the mainland and followed the Amazon and its tributaries, studying native peoples, their languages and customs, and local fauna and flora. His energy and skill won him the name of the Brazilian Humboldt. From 1793 until his death he directed Lisbon's natural history cabinet and botanical garden, though most exploration records vanished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-de-za: Alfonso de Zamora was a converted Spanish rabbi, baptized in 1506 and dead in 1531. He revised the Hebrew text for Cardinal Ximenes's Polyglot Bible, translated the Chaldee paraphrase in it, and added its sixth volume. He also published his Hebrew Introductions at Alcalá in 1526. His work served the great polyglot Bible project centred at Alcalá.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvaro-de-men:
Alvaro de Mendaña de Neyra, Spanish navigator born at Saragossa in 1541, died at Santa Cruz in the Solomon Islands on 18 October 1596. About 1558 he went to Lima at his uncle Lope García de Castro's invitation, the Viceroy, who equipped a two-ship expedition under his nephew. Sailing from Callao in November 1567, they discovered several Oceanic islands within about a year and returned to Peru in 1568.

His glowing description named them the Solomon Islands, supposing Solomon drew temple gold there. Later reports of wealth prompted a colonizing expedition under Philip II's order, sailing 11 April 1595. It discovered the Marquesas, named for the Viceroy of Peru's marquis wife, later called Nukahiva by Cook in 1774. Mendaña died before the voyage's end, delegating power to his resolute wife, who led the expedition safely to Manila in February 1596.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amadia-and-ak:
Amadia and Akra name two Chaldean Rite Catholic dioceses in Kurdistan, Turkey in Asia. Amadia first existed under another title, taking its present name only after the city of Amadia's foundation. Early in the nineteenth century the territory split into three dioceses: Amadia, Zakho, and Akra, each centred on its own town.

On 10 June 1895 the Dioceses of Amadia and Akra provisionally united, the bishop residing sometimes in one town, sometimes the other, or even at Araden. The provisional union joined two small towns under one bishop, who also sometimes resided at Araden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amra:
Amra is the name of certain ancient Irish elegies, or praise poems, written for native saints. The most famous survivor, the Amra of Columkille, reached print with a translation by O'Beirne Crowe in 1871. Later editors, including Atkinson and Whitley Stokes, worked from imperfect copies until Stokes edited the Bodleian text with a fresh translation.

Tradition says Dallan Mac Forgaill, chief poet of his day, composed the poem about 575. He wrote in thanks for Columkille saving the bards from expulsion at the assembly of Druim Cetta. Stokes and Strachan, judging by language rather than legend, place the poem in its present form near 800. Dallan also wrote an Amra on Senan and another on Conall of Ineskeel, with whom he shared a grave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anaphora:
A word from Greek for offering or sacrifice, anaphora belongs to the liturgy of the Greek Rite. There it names the part of the service that matches the Latin Canon of the Mass. The same word also covers the offering of Eucharistic bread, the large veil that covers it, and the procession that bears the offering to the altar.

Unlike the Roman Canon, which has stayed fixed from time immemorial, Greek anaphoras are many, though in substance they reach back to apostolic times. Their present shape dates from the late fourth or early fifth century. Basil the Great and John Chrysostom then shortened a liturgy grown long and tiring. Offertory here runs as a solemn procession, with priest, deacon, acolytes, and censer bearers carrying bread and wine through the small door of the icon screen. The article stresses what this antiquity proves about the sacrificial character of the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Skara, the most ancient diocese in Sweden, stood suffragan to Hamburg, then Lund, then Upsala from 1164 to 1530. It covered Skaraborg, Elfsborg, and Vermland, founded about 990 at Skara, capital of the Goths. It embraced all Gauthiod until about 1100, when its eastern part became Linkoping. At first missionary bishops preached wherever they pleased.

Odinkar Hvite the Elder was apparently the first bishop stationed at Skara about 990. Yet a bishop list from about 1325 names Sigurd, court bishop to King Olaf Tryggveson, as first bishop. Sigurd founded three churches in Vestergotland and baptized Olaf Skotkonung, first Christian king of Sweden, at Husaby in 1008. Thurgaut followed as first diocesan bishop, about 1012 to 1030. His nominal successor Gotskalk, a monk of Luneburg, never left his abbey. The cathedral was restored in 1312 to 1320 and painted in fresco. Bryniolph III settled the Lund frontier, and Vincent Hennings was beheaded by Christian II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancyra:
Today's Angora is the ancient Ancyra, a titular see of Galatia in Asia Minor, suffragan to Laodicea. Legend credits Midas with its founding, and about 277 before Christ it became a chief place of the Gallic conquerors of Asia Minor. Under the empire it grew into a centre of great trade. Gams gives its episcopal list, and that of a second Ancyra in Phrygia Pacatiana.

Ancyra's fame rests above all on the Monumentum Ancyranum, the official record of the Acts of Augustus, cut in marble on an ancient temple's walls. Scholars have copied and edited it several times since the sixteenth century. Its ruins still yield valuable bas-reliefs, inscriptions, and other building fragments, keeping the city rich ground for students of the ancient world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angora:
Angora is an Armenian rite diocese in Asia Minor, in Asiatic Turkey. Europeans call it Angora, the Turks Enguru, the ancient Galatian capital known as Ancyra. Midas was its founder, and Alexander marched triumphally through it. Under the Seleucid king Antiochus III, it temporarily lost its freedom. It was capital of the Galatian kings Dejotarus and Amyntas.

When Amyntas died in 25 B.C., it became Roman, flourishing under Augustus. The Byzantines let the Persians capture it in 619. Later Arabs ravaged it, then Konia Seljukids dispossessed them. Though taken by the Crusaders, it fell to Sultan Mourad in 1362. Since then it has remained Ottoman, except after the battle of 2 July 1402. The Armenian Catholic community has a bishop, 2 churches, 1 monastery, and schools for boys and girls. The Protestant Armenians have 1 church, an American Board station directed from Caesarea. The little Latin colony, drawn by the railway, is visited by Assumption Augustinians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angra:
Angra do Heroismo is the name of Angra, the Azores' episcopal see, suffragan of Lisbon. Paul III created it in 1534, and it stood vacant from 1637 to 1671. It sits on Terceira island. Besides Terceira, it covers Sao Jorge, Graciosa, Fayal, and Pico. Flores, Corvo, Sao Miguel, and Santa Maria complete the group.

Nearly all of its 262,073 people are Catholic. Its clergy and churches number 353 priests across 108 parishes, with 41 succursal or mission churches among 332 churches and chapels. Battandier's Annuaire Pontifical Catholique (1905) and Werner's Orbis Terrarum Catholicus (1890) supply these figures, which describe a diocese covering nine islands, nearly wholly Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ann-lobera:
Ann of Jesus, the Venerable Ann of Jesus, was a Carmelite nun and companion of Teresa, born in 1545, died in 1621. Daughter of Diego de Lobera and Francisca de Torres, she was deaf-mute until seven. Orphaned, she lived with relatives. After vowing virginity, she took the habit in 1570. Still a novice, Teresa called her to Salamanca over the novices. She professed in 1571 and accompanied Teresa to Beas in 1575, becoming its first prioress.

Later she founded at Granada. A misunderstanding with Teresa drew rebukes. With John of the Cross's help, constitutions were confirmed. Doria punished her for appealing to the Holy See. For three years she lost communion, intercourse, and active and passive voice. After this penance she was Salamanca prioress. A movement to bring the Teresian nuns to France carried her to Paris. She remained Brussels prioress for life. Miracles followed her death, and she was declared Venerable in 1878.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipater-of-:
Antipater of Bostra, in Arabia, was a fifth-century Greek prelate, among the foremost of the Roman Orient, flourishing about 460. He stood out as an opponent of Origen. Almost nothing is known of his life, apart from the high esteem in which contemporaries, civil and ecclesiastical, held him. The Seventh General Council's Fathers count him among authoritative ecclesiastical writers.

Only a few fragments of his long refutation of the Apology for Origen survive, in the acts of that council. Pamphilus and Eusebius of Caesarea had put that Apology together about 309. Antipater's work was seen as a masterly composition, and as late as 540 churches of the East were ordered to read it as an antidote to spreading Origenistic heresies. Against the Apollinarists he wrote a treatise, of which only brief fragments are known, plus several homilies, two of which survive whole. His memory is kept on 13 June.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-ferre:
Lisbon poet Antonio Ferreira, born in 1528 and dead of plague there in 1569, matters both for lyric verse and for drama in Portuguese letters. He studied law at Coimbra, reading classical poetry as eagerly as legal codes, and rose to judge of the Supreme Court at Lisbon, close to the court of John III. Unlike most Portuguese poets of his day, he never wrote in Spanish, keeping always to his native tongue while joining the reform of literary taste.

Like Sá de Miranda, he left old native forms behind to advance the Renaissance, the revival of classical learning and art, showing skill with the Italian eleven-syllable line. Sonnet, elegy, idyll, verse letter, and ode all came under his hand, fed by study of Italian Renaissance poets and Greek and Latin masters. His dramatic work is where his fame chiefly rests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-vieir:
Portuguese Jesuit Antonio Vieira, born at Lisbon in 1608 and dead at Bahia in 1697, combined missionary work, diplomacy, and oratory in one long career. Taken as a child to Bahia, he was schooled by the Jesuits, joined the Society in 1623, and was ordained in 1635, astonishing hearers at once with eloquence. When the Dutch besieged Bahia in 1640, his discourse for the success of Portuguese arms was called by the sceptic Raynal the most extraordinary burst of Christian eloquence.

After Portugal broke from Spain in 1640, Vieira went to Lisbon, became tutor to the Infante Dom Pedro, a court preacher, and member of the Royal Council. He worked in war and navy affairs, revived commerce, urged a national bank and a Brazilian trade company, and championed freedom for Indians and others. The entry traces a preacher who moved from pulpit to council chamber without leaving his missionary cause behind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-cam:
The Apostolic Camera was once the central board of finance for the papal government, once important in governing the States of the Church. Today it consists of the cardinal camerlengo, or chamberlain, the vice-camerlengo, an auditor, a general treasurer and seven chamber clerics. Since the States of the Church ceased to exist, papal income now comes chiefly from Peter's pence, offerings of the faithful. The Camera has lost practical importance as a finance board.

Peter's pence is handled by a special commission, and the Camera's officials hold what are in reality honorary offices. The camerlengo's chief duties fall during a vacancy of the Holy See, when he holds a share of papal authority. The vice-camerlengo, once governor of Rome charged with peace and order, still ranks first in authority during a vacancy. The entry charts an office fading from government to ceremony.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aymara:
The Aymara are a tribe of Indians living in northern Bolivia, the eastern Andes slopes, and the Peruvian districts around Lake Titicaca, save its northern tip, held by Quichua speakers. Their numbers cannot be safely given, since three centuries of mixing blur the count. They certainly run to several thousands, counting mestizos living by Indian custom. The name Aymara fits their language, which seems allied to Quichua.

They are mountaineers of the tableland, the Puna, between the eastern Cordillera and the volcanic coast chain. They farm potatoes, quinua, and maize where altitude above twelve thousand feet allows. They raise llamas, alpacas, cattle, and donkeys, and work in towns as journeymen and on the lake shore as stevedores. They live in autonomous communities called estancias, choosing officers, hilacata and alcalde, for mostly one year, and they pay a per capita tax. Their idiom first appears in print in a 1583 catechism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balthasar-bar:
Balthasar Barreira was a Portuguese Jesuit missionary born at Lisbon in 1531, who died on Angola's mission in 1612. Angola, on Africa's southwest coast, was the scene of his life's labors. He spent his whole working life on that African mission. His writings consist chiefly of Relations sent to the Society of Jesus, describing the province's political and spiritual state.

He recounted in detail the Spaniards' 1583 victory, under Paul de Morales, over an army of native people. Accounts of pagan tribes converted and native kings baptized fill much of his work. Treatises on the people's manners and customs round out his principal subjects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belem-do-para:
Belém do Pará is a Brazilian archdiocese, suffragan of Bahia from 1719 and metropolitan from 3 May 1906. Its city, capital of Pará on the Bay of Guajara, bears the full name Santa Maria de Nazareth do Pará and was founded in 1615. It is South America's most northerly important port, nearest North America and Europe, and the great outlet for Pará's rubber and coffee.

The city holds 100,000 people, with exports near $25,000,000 and imports near $12,000,000 yearly. Its old Carmelite convent became a seminary, its Jesuit college now houses the episcopal palace and another seminary. The Amparo Orphan Asylum ranks among the state's leading charities, and the archdiocese counts about 480,000 Catholics. Its seventy-seven parishes are served by forty-seven secular and thirteen religious priests, with twenty-one brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-pere:
Benedict Pereira, a Jesuit philosopher, theologian, and Bible scholar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born near Valencia about 1535, he died at Rome in 1610 after joining the Jesuits in 1552. In Rome he taught literature, philosophy, theology, and Scripture in turn, and left eight printed works plus much manuscript.

His great work comments on Genesis in four volumes, tackling the Flood, Noah's ark, and the tower of Babel. The entry calls it a mine of learning, praised even by critical scholars of a later age. Other writings range over philosophy and the natural world, marking him as a wide-ranging Jesuit teacher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernhard-galu:
Bernhard Galura, Prince-Bishop of Brixen, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Herbolzheim in 1764, he died in 1856 after a formation broken by Joseph II's suppression of his first convent at Altbreisach. He entered the Freiburg seminary in 1783, took a doctorate in theology, and was ordained at Vienna in 1788.

Prefect of studies at Freiburg, then bishop, he guided Brixen through the Napoleonic storms and the restoration that followed. Writings on theology and church life accompanied his long episcopate, one of the longest of his age. The entry presents a steady bishop formed in an age of suppression and rebuilding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bostra:
Bostra, the Fortress, rose from a Nabataean town to metropolis of Roman Arabia under Trajan. It is not Bosor of Reuben nor Edom's Bosrah, but perhaps the Bosora taken by the Maccabees. When Cornelius Palma destroyed the Nabataean kingdom in 105 or 106, Bostra became Nova Trajana Bostra, home of the Third Cyrenaican Legion and start of the great road to the Red Sea.

Under Alexander Severus it became a Roman colony, and Ammianus called it a great city, with ruins suggesting some 80,000 people. Colonnades, arches, baths, a theatre, temples, and churches still stand. Mahomet visited it as a trade hub, Crusaders failed to take it, and an earthquake in 1151 left it ruined. Now Bosra Eski-Sham, it holds barely 1,000 people and a small Turkish garrison.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathedra:
A cathedra is the bishop's chair or throne in his cathedral, from which he presides at solemn functions. At first it sat mid-apse, with the benches of assisting priests on either side at a lower level. The same arrangement appears in catacomb frescoes of Christ enthroned among the apostles. The earliest thrones were high-backed armchairs rounded at the top, carved from a single block of marble.

Later forms varied. Wooden chairs were used in Africa. Some Roman basilicas cut a niche for the throne in the apse wall, and Monte Cassino keeps one with a perforated seat like those in Roman baths. The article surveys these forms and their decoration, and notes the related term faldstool for the portable seat used when a bishop officiates away from his throne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cestra:
Cestra was a titular see of Asia Minor placed by Hierocles, Georgius Cyprius, and Parthey's Notitiae episcopatuum in Isauria, under Seleucia. Epiphanius, its bishop, attended Chalcedon in 451 and signed the letter to Emperor Leo in 458. Another bishop, Elpidius, backed Severus.

Lequien guessed the town stood beside the River Cestros in Pamphylia, drawing its name from that stream. The article calls this guess inadmissible: it led the Gerarchia cattolica of 1895 to identify Cestra with Ak-Sou, which is the river's name, not a city's. The site itself has not yet been identified.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christina-ale:
An entry on Christina Alexandra, Queen of Sweden, daughter of Gustavus Adolphus, born at Stockholm in December 1626. Her father died in 1632, her mother had wished for a son, and the girl was raised by nurses, then by her aunt Catherine. By her father's command she was brought up like a boy, taught by distinguished men, and she mastered languages, history, and politics while scorning dress and feminine pastimes.

At eighteen she took up government in 1644, but she prized personal independence and leaned toward the Catholic Church. On 6 June 1654 at Uppsala she gave up the throne to her cousin Charles Gustavus and set out for Rome. There she prayed, aided the poor, collected books and art, and made her palace a centre for scholars and artists. She died at Rome in April 1689, a devout Catholic to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cibyra:
An entry on Cibyra, a titular see in Caria, Asia Minor, founded by the Lycian district of the Solymi. It led the Kabalian tetrapolis with two votes, could field 30,000 foot and 2,000 horse, and was ruled by its own kings in 190 before Christ. Rome let it stay independent with its territory in 130, but Murena, Sulla's lieutenant, joined it to the province of Asia in 84, making it capital of the Cibyratic district.

Cibyra was famed for ironwork, yet off the great trade routes it lost its early prosperity. After an earthquake, Tiberius restored it; it struck coins and dated its own era from the year 25. Justinian joined it to Caria, and it appears as suffragan to Stauropolis from the seventh century. Six bishops are listed by Lequien, from Letodorus at Nicaea in 325 to Stephen, a partisan of Photius who retracted in 869. Its ruins stand near Horzoum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coimbra:
Eduardo de Hinojosa y Naveros traces the diocese of Coimbra in Portugal. It stands as suffragan of Braga, in the province of Beira. Its first known bishop, Lucentius, attended the first council of Braga in 563. Titular bishops kept the line alive through the Arab conquest. The see was restored in 1088, after Christians retook the city in 1064. Later bishops include Pedro, chancellor of King Diniz. They also include Manoel de Menezes, who fell with Dom Sebastian at Kassr-el-Kaber.

Coimbra's old cathedral rose in the first half of the twelfth century, partly at Bishop Miguel's cost. It stands as a fine Romanesque monument. The newer Renaissance cathedral from 1580 draws less praise. Santa Cruz monastery, founded in 1131, once ranked among the kingdom's richest houses. In 1904 the diocese held 875,853 people in 308 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-el:
The Council of Elvira met at Elliberis near Granada early in the fourth century, and stands as the first known council in Spain. Nineteen bishops from across the peninsula attended, with twenty-six priests sitting beside them, though only bishops signed the acts. Its date stays disputed, with proposals ranging from about 300 to 324.

Eighty-one disciplinary canons cover marriage, baptism, idolatry, fasting, excommunication, cemeteries, usury, vigils, and dealings with pagans, Jews, and heretics. Canon thirty-three gives the oldest positive church rule on clerical celibacy, while canon thirty-six, barring pictures in churches, still sparks debate over image veneration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
The Councils of Ancyra, three fourth-century synods in Galatia's former capital, now Angora, trace orthodoxy and heresy across sixty years. The first, an orthodox plenary synod of 314, left twenty-five disciplinary canons, a key document for the early administration of penance. Nine canons set terms for reconciling the lapsi, Christians who had lapsed under persecution.

A Semi-Arian conciliabulum of 358, under Basil of Ancyra, condemned cruder Arian blasphemies yet taught the Son similar to the Father in all things, though different in substance. In 375 Arian bishops gathered at Ancyra again and removed several bishops from office, Gregory of Nyssa among them, closing a turbulent local record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-leopold:
This biographical entry follows Count Leopoldo Cicognara, an Italian politician, writer on art, and collector. He was born at Ferrara in 1767 and died at Venice in 1834. Bonaparte's campaigns and hopes for Italian renewal drew him into public life. He served the Cisalpine Republic at Milan and Turin, sat at the Congress of Lyons, and survived imprisonment and exile in a conspiracy case.

Retiring from politics at thirty-eight, he gave himself to the fine arts. He directed the new Academy of Fine Arts at Venice until 1827, and built its museum much as it stands today. His three-volume history of sculpture, with 131 plates, aimed to complete Winckelmann. His late passion for rare engravings left a collection of over three thousand fifteenth- and sixteenth-century prints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cybistra:
A short entry describes Cybistra, a Cappadocian titular see in Asia Minor. Ptolemy places it in Lycaonia, Strabo in Cilicia, and Cicero in Cappadocia at the edge of Cilicia near Mount Taurus. It appears as a suffragan of Tyana in the Synecdemus of Hierocles and early lists of bishoprics.

Harun captured it in 805, Almamun in 832, it probably became an independent archbishopric in the eleventh century and stayed Byzantine after much of Cappadocia fell to the Turks. Nearby stood the fortress Heracleia, later united with Cybistra in one bishopric, its name surviving as modern Eregli. Five bishops are quoted by Lequien, from Nicaea in 325 to Constantinople late in the twelfth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniele-da-vo:
A biographical entry follows Daniele da Volterra, born Ricciarelli at Volterra in 1509 and dead at Rome in 1566. As a boy he entered the Siena studios of Sodoma and Peruzzi. Finding little welcome, he left for Rome. There Michelangelo befriended him, aiding commissions and ideas, above all for paintings in the Trinita dei Monti chapel.

His Descent from the Cross was once ranked with Raphael's Transfiguration and Domenichino's Last Communion among Rome's most famous pictures. His chief work, the Murder of the Innocents, now hangs in the Uffizi. Commissioned by Paul IV to drape the nude figures in Michelangelo's Last Judgment, he earned the nickname Breeches Maker. His Victory of David over Goliath was long attributed to Michelangelo himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dansara:
A short entry describes Dansara, a titular see in Osrhoene. Stephanus of Byzantium mentions it as a town near Edessa, and Procopius counts it among the castles around Theodosiopolis fortified by Justinian. Probably then it became a bishopric suffragan to Edessa, appearing in the Antiochene list of bishoprics under Patriarch Anastasius.

Its bishop Nonnus attended the Fifth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople in 553. No other bishop is known, and the see must have vanished with the Arab invasions. Whether it still existed in the tenth century is uncertain. Its site has never been identified. The name is often written Dausara, while forms such as Lansara are wrong, and the Latin titular see was recently suppressed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-debbora:
A scriptural entry presents Debbora, prophetess and judge, wife of Lapidoth. God endowed her with prophetic gifts that won her veneration and great authority among divided Israelite tribes. Her wisdom first showed in settling disputes. She sat under her palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in Mount Ephraim, and Israel came to her for judgment.

Other judges in the book are mainly deliverers and leaders. But Debbora's trusted judgments enabled her to free a nation oppressed twenty years by Canaanites under Sisara. His nine hundred iron chariots dominated the plain of Esdraelon. At God's word she summoned Barak of Kedesh to lead Israel's army. The victory that followed, celebrated in her song, brought forty years of peace and lasting fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diaspora:
Diaspora is a Greek word for scattering. It named the lands outside Palestine where Jews lived in exile, and then the scattered Jews themselves. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows the term from the Greek Old Testament, where the scattering of Israel stands as punishment for turning away from God. New Testament letters were also sent to believers of the dispersion.

Each invasion of Palestine brought fresh deportations, and these drove the scattering wider. The entry traces how exiled groups kept their faith and built houses of worship in Roman cities. Spread across many lands, they stayed tied by law, worship, and hope of return.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dora:
Dora was a titular see of Palestina Prima, its Semitic name meaning dwelling or abode. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how its king joined the league against Joshua and fell with the confederates. The town was first allotted to Asher, then given to Manasses, who failed to drive out the people and set them to tribute. The Israelites may have held only the upper city, called Nafat Dor.

The Egyptian king Rameses the Third planted a Phoenician colony there, drawn, says Stephan of Byzantium, by shells yielding the famed Tyrian purple dye. Dora later passed through many hands, and recent settlers have built nearby. The entry draws on Guerin and the Palestine survey to fix this small port on the map of Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-drusipara:
Drusipara was a titular see in Thracia Prima, a town of unknown ancient history on the road from Adrianople to Byzantium. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that Saint Alexander suffered martyrdom there under Maximian. Under the emperor Maurice the Khakan of the Avars seized the city, burned the church, and destroyed the martyr's relics. At first a suffragan of Heraclea, it rose in the eighth and ninth centuries to an independent archbishopric.

Bulgarian invasions likely ended that rank. Mesene appears in later lists as Drusipara's new name. At Mesene in 1453, the wife of Grand Duke Notaras died. Today Mesene is a small village of five hundred souls east of Karishtiran, a quiet end for a martyr's town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ekkehard-of-a:
Ekkehard of Aura was a Benedictine monk and chronicler born about 1050 and dead after 1125, of whom little is known. About 1101 he made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, and in 1106 he sat at the Council of Guastalla. He seems to have belonged first to Saint Michael's at Bamberg. Then he became abbot of Aura on the Franconian Saale, founded by Bishop Otto of Bamberg under the rule of Hirschau.

His Chronicon Universale is the chief source for German history from 1080 to 1125. In five books it runs from Creation to the building of Rome. Then it goes to the birth of Christ, to Charlemagne, and to the opening of Henry V's reign. The last book covers that reign itself. The work blends older writings and continuations, and scholars trace much of it to Frutolf of Saint Michael's. Ekkehard's own share is the account of Henry V.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-esdras-ezra:
Esdras, or Ezra, was a priest and scribe of Israel's restoration after the Exile. The chief sources for his life are Esdras and Nehemias. Apocryphal writings also concern him, but they relate legendary tales of a later age and can hardly be relied upon. Esdras was of priestly descent, in the line of Sardoc. He is known rather as scribe than priest: a ready scribe in the law of Moses, qualified for his task among his people.

The relation of Esdras's work to Nehemias's is among the most mooted questions of the Restoration. Many scholars hold, from the traditional order of the text, that Esdras came before Nehemias. Others, including Van Hoonacker, Cheyne, and Kent, hold that Nehemias came first. The former view dates Esdras's coming about 458 before Christ; the opposite opinion, as late as 397.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evora:
Evora is a Portuguese city and archbishopric whose history runs from Roman times to the modern age. Julius Caesar gave it the name Liberalitas Julia, and inscriptions and coins attest its high rank among the towns of Roman Spain. Its bishop Quintianus sat at Elvira's council early in the fourth century. The list of his successors breaks for two centuries. It then runs from King Reccared in 586 to the Arab invasion of 714. After that almost nothing is known for four and a half centuries save the epitaph of a Bishop Daniel of January 1100.

Alfonso I retook the city in 1166, and after passing through the hands of Braga, Compostella, and Lisbon, Evora was raised to an archbishopric in 1544. Among its famed prelates were Enrique, who founded its university and ruled Portugal as king from 1578, and Teotonio de Braganza. Others were Alfonso de Portugal and Father Manuel de Cenaculo Villasboas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ex-cathedra:
Ex Cathedra, literally from the chair, is a theological term for authoritative teaching, applied above all to definitions of the Roman pontiff. Cathedra first meant the seat of a professor or bishop, then came to mean the teaching office itself. Its present meaning was fixed by the Vatican Council in its fourth session, in the constitution on the Church of Christ, chapter four.

That decree teaches it as a divinely revealed dogma that when the Roman pontiff speaks ex cathedra, he is infallible. He must act as pastor and doctor of all Christians, by his supreme apostolic authority. He must define a doctrine on faith or morals for the whole Church to hold, with the divine help promised to him in Blessed Peter. Such definitions are therefore irreformable on their own, not by the Church's consent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exedra:
Exedra is an architectural term with several linked senses. First it means a semicircular seat of stone or marble, or a rectangular or semicircular recess. It also means the portico of the Greek palaestra, where learned men held disputations. In private houses it meant the vestibule used for talk.

The term is also used for a porch or chapel jutting out from a larger building. As a synonym for cathedra, it can mean a throne or seat of any kind. It can mean a small private chamber as well. Last, it can mean the space between an oriel window and small chapels between a church's buttresses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fajardo-diego:
Diego de Saavedra Fajardo was a Spanish diplomat and political writer. Born in 1584, he studied law at Salamanca before entering royal service. He served as secretary and successor to Cardinal Borgia at Rome. Philip IV then used him as a diplomat for some thirty-five years.

His best-known work is Idea de un principe, printed in 1670. It sets out, through emblems and comment, how a Christian prince should rule. Fajardo also wrote on the Goths and on European politics. He died in 1648, and the book reached print after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feliz-de-azar:
Feliz de Azara was a Spanish soldier, engineer, and keen naturalist. Born in Aragon in 1746, he rose to the rank of brigadier general. Sent to South America in 1781, he helped settle limits between Portuguese and Spanish lands. He stayed there until 1801, studying the life and habits of mammals and birds.

Azara observed quadrupeds' habits rather than their anatomy or physiology alone. His notes reached Paris and appeared in print at Paris in 1801. A fuller Spanish work on Paraguay's quadrupeds followed at Madrid in 1802. He criticised Jesuit methods with Indians, showing little understanding of native character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernando-de-h:
Fernando de Herrera was a Spanish lyric poet and head of a Seville school. Born in 1537, he led a school of lyric poets there. A disciple of Garcilaso, he perfected his master's form and added pathos and dignity. His martial odes on Lepanto rank among the classics of Spanish literature.

Herrera, called the divine, sang in Petrarchian strains of his love for Eliodora. He took minor orders, likely to enjoy ecclesiastical benefices. His Anotaciones on Garcilaso show genuine critical acumen and learning. He published only part of his verse in his own lifetime.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferrara:
Ferrara is a rich Italian archdiocese on the Po di Volano, immediately subject to Rome. The Este family ruled it as the pope's lieges until 1598. Alfonso I and II generously patronised Tasso, Ariosto, Boiardo, and Guarini. Its famous university, founded in 1391, drew scholars from far and wide.

In 1598 Clement VIII brought the town directly under papal rule. French troops held it in 1796, and the Kingdom of Italy annexed it in 1859. The Council of Ferrara opened there on 8 January 1438. Greek and Latin bishops met to seek reunion as the only defence against the Turks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flaminius-ann:
Flaminius Annibali de Latera was an Italian Franciscan historian born at Latera in 1733. He entered the Observants at sixteen, taught theology in several convents, and served as definitor general. When Napoleon suppressed the Italian convents in 1810, he retired to Viterbo, dying there in 1813. He wrote for fifty years, mostly with a polemical motive amid fierce Franciscan controversies.

His chief works supplemented Sbaralea's Bullarium and defended the Portiuncula indulgence and the stigmata. He answered attacks on the Stations of the Cross and wrote lives of Colette and Hyacintha Mariscotti. His four-volume survey of religious orders appeared in 1790 and 1791, with a second edition in 1796. He also worked on the Franciscan Breviary and wrote a history of the Farnese house of the former city of Castro.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-her:
Francisco Herrera the Elder, born at Seville in 1576 and dead at Madrid in 1656. He was a Spanish painter, etcher, medallist, and architect who pioneered the bold, natural style that Velazquez would perfect. Trained by Luis Fernandez, he broke from the timid style and Italian ways of his day, first using long brushes that help explain his modern, dexterous handling. Many authorities credit him with founding the Spanish School. His passionate temper and rough manners drove away many pupils, including the thirteen-year-old Velazquez after a year.

Skilled in bronze, he engraved medals so well that he was charged with counterfeiting and fled to the Jesuit college, where he painted The Triumph of St. Hermengild. It so impressed Philip IV in 1621 that the king pardoned him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-lop:
Francisco Lopez de Gomara, born at Seville in 1510, studied at Alcala, was ordained priest, travelled to Rome, and on his return in 1540 became private chaplain to Hernando Cortes. He accompanied Cortes on the Algerian expedition, was at Valladolid in 1556 or 1557 after his patron's death, and is thought to have retired to Seville, where he probably died. From Cortes and other returned conquerors he gathered the material for his great history, though he never crossed to America himself.

His Hispania Victrix, the first and second parts of the General History of the Indies, was published at Saragossa in 1552. It covers the discovery and conquest of the Antilles, Peru, Chile, and Central America, Magellan's voyage, and the conquest of Mexico and New Spain to 1551. Translated into French, Italian, and Mexican, it won readers by a concise, graceful style, but Bernal Diaz del Castillo wrote his True History to refute it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriello-chi:
Gabriello Chiabrera, a poet born at Savona in 1552, was called the Italian Pindar for his classical lyrics. Sent to Rome at nine to live with an uncle, he studied philosophy at the Jesuit college and moved among the learned men of the day. Dukes, popes, and the Republic of Genoa sought his favor. He spent most of his life between Florence and Genoa and married at fifty.

Chiabrera took Pindar, Anacreon, Alcaeus, and Horace as models, seeking, as he said, a new world of poetry like Columbus. He fought the stale Petrarchism of his age and led toward the classical lyric of the next century. Though he claimed to scorn rhyme, he mastered it and coined new meters. His lyrics, graceful yet cool, are the part of his work still read today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gadara:
Gadara, a titular see of Palaestina Prima, is a place scholars cannot pin down with confidence. Two sees bore the name, one in each Palestine, so known bishops cannot always be assigned to the right city. The Gadara of this article, in the first Palestine, has never been identified on the ground.

Candidates crowd the field: a Gader whose king Joshua defeated, now Djédur between Bethlehem and Hebron, and a Gedera of the Shephelah plain, now Khirbet-Djedireh or Qatrah. Perhaps neither is the true Gadara. It can hardly be Gazara, or Gezer, the well-known scriptural city near Amwas, though the match is often claimed. The entry leaves the riddle open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gangra:
Gangra, a titular see in Paphlagonia whose native name means goat, still grazes great herds today. Once part of Galatia, it served as capital of King Dejotarus, friend of Rome and foe of Mithridates, then rose to metropolis of its province. Le Quien lists twenty-two archbishops across the fourth to twelfth centuries, none of great note.

Gangra's chief Christian moment came with its council, probably in 343, against Eustathius of Armenia and his extreme asceticism. More than twenty canons defended lawful marriage against his disciples' scorn. Turks took the land in the fourteenth century, Tamerlane seized the town in 1402, and Murad II retook it in 1423. Now called Tchiangre, it holds 16,000 souls, its old cathedral of Saint Demetrius a mosque.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gargara:
Gargara, a titular see in Asia Minor under Ephesus, stood on Mount Gargaron, the highest peak of fabled Mount Ida. Colonists from Assos first held it, followed by folk from Miletopolis, and the grammarian Diotimes kept a school there poorly attended by its rough people. Three ancient bishops are known: John in 518, Theodore in 553, and Ephrem in 878.

The mountain, now Dikeli-Dagh in the Kaz range, keeps the old Ida name, and ruins at Akrili may mark the city itself. Readers must not mix Gargara with Gargar, the Jacobite bishopric west of the Euphrates near Malatia, now Gerger. The entry is short, but it fixes place, bishops, and a common confusion with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Caprara was a statesman and cardinal born at Bologna in 1733, who died at Paris in 1810. Taking his mother's name, he served as vice-legate of Ravenna, nuncio at Cologne, Lucerne, and Vienna, and was made cardinal in 1792. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a courteous diplomat whom Napoleon chose as legate precisely because he expected little resistance.

As legate a latere in France from August 1801, Caprara oversaw the execution of the Concordat. He officiated at the restoration of public worship in Notre-Dame on Easter Day 1802. He bent too far toward the constitutional bishops, against Rome's orders, yet in 1803 he protested fiercely against the Organic Articles. Made Archbishop of Milan in 1802, he blessed Napoleon's Iron Crown in 1805 and left his fortune to a Milan hospital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-goajira:
Goajira is the most northern portion of South America, a peninsula running into the Caribbean Sea. Awarded to Colombia on arbitration in 1891 after a dispute with Venezuela, it joined the State of Magdalena. A Catholic Encyclopedia article counts its people at eighty thousand, fifty thousand of them Catholics, mostly of Indian or mixed race.

The peninsula covers about 5500 square miles, with very high temperatures on the plains and temperate mountains. It has a good supply of cabinet wood but not much trade. The Capuchins in charge of the missions have converted large numbers among a people once very intractable. Erected as a vicariate Apostolic by Pius X in 1905, it holds sixteen Capuchin priests, twenty churches and chapels, and seven schools with three hundred children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guadalajara:
Mexico's Archdiocese of Guadalajara was cut from Michoacán by Paul III in 1548, with its seat first at Compostela and moved to Guadalajara in 1560. Its cathedral, begun in 1571 and dedicated in 1618, holds a celebrated Murillo painting, and the entry moves bishop by bishop through the see's first three and a half centuries.

Felipe Galindo y Chávez founded the seminary in 1699, Antonio Alcalde founded a university and a hospital for 500 sick poor and fed crowds in the famine of 1786. Pedro Loza ordained 536 priests and started free parish primary schools. Liberal suppression of the convents, the Jesuits' return in 1906, and a seminary of 1,000 students round out a diocese of about 1,200,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guilo-cesare-:
Piedmont Jesuit Giulio Cesare Cordara, born at Alessandria in 1704, joined the Society at fourteen and became a historian, poet, and satirist of wide fame. A discourse on Gregory XIII and a satire on the Cabalists won him a place among the Arcadians. His allegorical drama for the exiled Stuarts in Rome brought him their favour.

His satires on the literary spirit of his times, first published in 1737, pilloried self-appointed censors of taste. His Latin History of the Society of Jesus, covering the generalate of Mutius Vitelleschi from 1616 to 1633, is praised for elegance and dignity. After the suppression he withdrew to Turin and Alessandria, kept writing past eighty, and left more than sixty works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hauara:
Palestine's Hauara, a titular see suffragan of Petra, is a place whose site scholars cannot pin down, though its name survives in maps and lists. Peutinger's map sets it thirty-eight miles from Petra, Ptolemy and the Notitia Dignitatum mention it, the last noting a garrison of native horse archers. It lay somewhere between Aila and Petra.

It must not be confused with Stephen of Byzantium's Hauara, the Greeks' Leuke Kome harbour on the Red Sea, nor with Haura, a Jacobite see in Mesopotamia. It never had a bishop of its own in the old lists and does not appear in any episcopal Notitiae, so even the date it became a titular see is unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ibarra:
Ibarra is a diocese in southern Ecuador, suffragan to Quito, created by Pius IX in December 1862 from the provinces of Carchi and Imbabura, formerly in Quito's archdiocese. Francesco Jabani, apostolic delegate, named the exiled bishop of Antioquia, Antonio Riaño, as executor, and canonical erection followed in August 1865.

Riaño administered the diocese for two months, Arsenio Andrade, later bishop of Riobamba, and José María Jerovi, later archbishop of Quito, succeeded him. In April 1867 José Ignacio Checa y Barbo became first bishop of Ibarra, but moved to Quito in June 1868. Tomás Antonio Iturralde followed in 1869 and resigned in 1875, and the next two bishops, the Gonzálezes, both later became archbishops of Quito.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ibora:
Ibora was a titular see in Helenopont, suffragan to Amasia, whose primitive name was Gaziura, once a royal city mentioned by Strabo as deserted. A Greek inscription from Mithridates of Pontus's time was found on its fortress rock, and a rock-hewn gallery descends inside the mountain, perhaps a secret store for royal treasures.

Evagrius Ponticus, the famous fourth-century Origenist ascetic, was a native of Ibora. Nearby lay Annesi, St. Basil's property, where he lived a religious life on the Iris with Gregory and his sister Macrina, and their letters mention Ibora often. Procopius says an earthquake destroyed it in the sixth century. Le Quien names seven bishops from the fourth to ninth centuries, and the see still existed about 1170. Today it is called Turkhal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isaura:
Capital of the Isaurian tribes, a tough and raiding people, Isaura stood even before Alexander's expedition and paid dearly for its stubbornness. Rather than fall to the Greek generals Perdiccas and Philip, its people after desperate resistance buried themselves under their city's ruins, as Diodorus tells it. Rebuilt, the city was destroyed again by Servilius, then handed to Amyntas, last king of Galatia, who tried in 25 before Christ to make it his capital.

Strabo, the source for these turns, speaks of two cities in his day, Old Isaura and New Isaura, and the record fits. In 266 a usurper named Trebellian made Isaura his capital and was killed the next year, while Ammianus in the fourth century calls the city ruined. New Isaura survives as Dorla in the Konya region. The entry packs siege, rebuilding, and ruin into one see's history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste-François Pitra, a French cardinal, archaeologist, and theologian born in 1812 and dead at Rome in 1889, showed tireless learning from youth. Schooled at Autun and ordained in 1836, he taught rhetoric there before joining the Benedictines at Solesmes in 1842.

Pitra's first triumph came in 1839, when he read the broken Autun inscription, a third-century epitaph whose opening verses spell the Greek word for fish. He saw in it early witness to baptism, the Eucharist, prayer for the dead, and life everlasting. Later work on ancient liturgy and church documents made him one of the most learned churchmen of his age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joachim-of-fl:
Joachim of Flora, a Cistercian abbot and mystic born near Cosenza about 1132 and dead in Calabria in 1202. He was placed young at the Norman Sicilian court by his notary father. On pilgrimage to the Holy Land some great calamity, perhaps plague, turned him from the world, and he spent a whole Lent in prayer on Mount Tabor.

Back in Italy Joachim joined Sambucina, preached as a layman, then took the Cistercian habit at Corazzo and was ordained about 1168. Elected abbot against his will, he begged Lucius III in 1182 to free him from temporal care. He spent his last years at Casamari writing his three great books on Scripture's hidden sense, above all his pattern of three ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-maria-sa:
Juan María Salvatierra was an Italian-born Jesuit who founded the California missions. Born at Milan in 1648 to a Spanish family, he read a book on Indian missions at Parma's Jesuit college and resolved to give his life to them. He sailed to Mexico in 1675, labored ten years among the Tarahumara of Chihuahua, and became inspector of northern missions.

With Father Kino's encouragement, Salvatierra won authority in 1697 to evangelize Lower California at the missionaries' own cost. Landing at Concepción Bay that October with six soldiers, he founded Loreto, the first California mission, and then five more. Donations for the work formed the historic Pious Fund. He died at Guadalajara in 1717.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-junipero-serr:
Junípero Serra was the Franciscan who founded the first California missions and directed the chain northward. Born at Petra on Majorca in 1713, he entered the Franciscan Order in 1730 and later took a doctorate at Palma. He spent nine years among the Sierra Gorda missions, learned the Pame language, and translated the catechism into it. In 1767 he became superior of fifteen Franciscans assigned to the Indian missions of Lower California.

He reached San Diego on 1 July 1769 and founded its mission fifteen days later, the first of twenty-one missions. Others founded by him or under his direction included San Carlos, San Antonio, San Gabriel, and San Luis Obispo. San Francisco de Asís, San Juan Capistrano, Santa Clara, and San Buenaventura followed. In 1773 he carried his complaints against the military commander to the viceroy and won nearly every point of his thirty-two articles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jusepe-de-rib:
Jusepe de Ribera, called Spagnoletto, the little Spaniard, was a painter whose name became tied to terrifying subjects. Born at Játiva in 1588, he studied under Ribalta at Valencia and reached Rome at eighteen, alone and without money. A Caravaggio picture drew his admiration, and he went to Naples seeking the artist, only to learn he had just died. By 1626 he lived at Naples like a nobleman, receiving viceroys and hosting traveling artists.

He could paint charming figures with a Correggio-like grace, yet he sought neither ugliness nor beauty for its own sake. His fixed idea was sensation: weather-beaten beggars, wasted anchorites, and parchment-like St. Jeromes show a ruined human body. The work answers the voluptuous paganism of the Renaissance with Catholic Reformation asceticism. His last years were clouded when Don Juan of Austria seduced his daughter; the story of his suicide is fiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kathleen-o-me:
Kathleen O'Meara (1839-1888) was a Dublin-born novelist and life-writer who spent most of her life in Paris. This entry covers six novels, the first issued under the pen name Grace Ramsey, plus the biographies that made her reputation.

Her fiction takes up poverty and suffering and answers them with Christian charity, in a warm and clean-toned style, and 'Narka, a Story of Russian Life' is judged her best novel. Biography was her real gift: lives of Madame Mohl and her Paris salon, Bishop Thomas Grant, Ozanam, and the Cure d'Ars, Jean-Baptiste Vianney, the last printed after her death. She also wrote for 'The Tablet' from Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-land-tenure-i:
Land-tenure in the Christian era asks how land was held and owned across nineteen hundred years of the Church's rise in Europe. The article insists on separating what records prove from what is doubtful and what is merely hypothetical.

Motive and attitude, it warns, are always disputable, while legal definitions and public acts stand on documents. Modern theory, its target, treats property as a mechanical state institution, not an extension of personality, dignity, and will rooted in man's nature and his Creator's purpose. Apologists as opposed as those praising property for spurring effort or rewarding cunning and those damning it as robbery share that theory, as does Ricardian rent analysis in stressing property's collective side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laura:
A laura, from a Greek word for a narrow way or passage, was a Palestinian monastery of the semi-eremitical type, known from the late fifth century. Later the word also meant a town quarter, as at Alexandria, matching the laura's shape: a ring of hermit cells around a central church.

Life there stood midway between pure hermit life and full community life. Each monk lived alone under a superior, joining common life only on Saturdays and Sundays for the solemn Eucharist. The central church became the coenobium, house of probation for future solitaries and refuge for those too weak for full rigour. St. Chariton, who died about 350, founded Pharan and Douka, while the Cappadocian Sabas founded Mar Saba in 483, the Great Laura, still bearing his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-limyra:
Limyra was a titular see of Lycia, a small city on Lycia's southern coast, on the Limyrus, twenty stadia from the river's mouth. Strabo, Ptolemy, and several Latin authors mention it. Its history is otherwise unknown, except that Caius Caesar, adopted son of Augustus, died there.

The Notitiae Episcopatuum list Limyra as a suffragan of Myra down to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, with six known bishops: Diotimus, mentioned by St. Basil; Lupicinus, present at Constantinople in 381; Stephen, at Chalcedon in 451; Theodore, at Constantinople in 553; Leo, at Nicaea in 787; and Nicephorus, at Constantinople in 879. Limyra's ruins lie three or four miles east of Fineka village, in Adalia's sanjak, Konia's vilayet, and comprise a theatre, tombs, sarcophagi, bas-reliefs, plus Greek and Lycian inscriptions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucera:
Lucera is an ancient Apulian diocese and city, first Daunian, then Roman from 320 BC, with a colony planted in 314. Samnites beat Rome nearby in 294, and Pompey's men held it as a strongpoint against Caesar.

Frederick II moved Sicily's Saracens here, and they became his loyal troops against popes and barons, with the royal treasury housed in town. Charles of Anjou met long resistance, and in 1300 the remaining Saracens were converted en masse, their mosque giving way to the cathedral of St. Mary of Victory. Bishops from Marcus about 743 through Gasotti, Acerno, and Bozzuti fill the later record, with Montecorvino joined in 1818.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lystra:
Lystra is a titular see in Lycaonia, suffragan of Iconium, famous from Paul's first visit. He healed a lame man, and the crowd, mistaking him for Jupiter and Barnabas for Mercury, tried to sacrifice to them. The apostles stopped them with difficulty, yet the same folk, stirred by Jews from Iconium, later stoned Paul.

Paul returned at least twice, built a Christian community there, and won Timothy, son of a Jewish mother and pagan father, as his disciple. Pliny puts Lystra in Galatia, Ptolemy in Isauria, Acts in Lycaonia. Its site is found at Khatum Serai, twelve miles south of Iconium, marked by ruins and five bishops named between the fourth and ninth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mandaurus-or-:
Madaura, also called Mandaurus, was a titular see of Numidia and an old Numidian town. It had belonged to King Syphax, then passed to Massinissa after the Second Punic War. It became a Roman colony near the end of the first century and won fame for its schools.

Apuleius, author of The Golden Ass, was born there, as were the grammarians Nonius and Maximus. St Augustine studied there, and a later letter of his shows many townsfolk still pagan. Yet Madaura had many martyrs, known by epitaphs and named in the Roman martyrology for 4 July. Three bishops stand on record: Antigonus at Carthage in 349, Placentius in 407 and 411, and Pudentius, exiled by Huneric after the conference of 484. Its ruins near Mdaourouch in Algeria show a fine mausoleum, vast baths, a Byzantine fortress, and a Christian basilica.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcellus-of-:
Marcellus of Ancyra was a bishop at the Councils of Ancyra and Nicaea. He fought Arianism with vigour. In his zeal he swung to the opposite extreme, a softened Sabellianism. He was condemned several times and died deprived of his see about 374.

Soon after Nicaea he wrote against Asterius, a leading Arian. He held that the three persons were only a passing order. God began as one person alone. At creation the Word went forth as God's action in the world, became flesh in Christ, and so became Son. The Holy Ghost went forth third. At the end of all things, Christ and the Spirit would return to the Father, and God would be one again. Jerusalem condemned his works, Constantinople deposed him in 336, Rome under Julius I cleared him in 340, and he held Ancyra again briefly before a final deposition about 353.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-del-ba:
Martin Del Barco Centenera was born at Logrono in 1535 and died about 1602. He became a secular priest and in 1572 sailed as chaplain with Juan Ortiz de Zarate's expedition to the Rio de la Plata. For twenty-four years he shared Spanish exploration in the Argentine with fearless courage and became archdeacon of Paraguay's church.

Back in Europe he finished his poem La Argentina, dedicated to Portugal's viceroy for Philip III of Spain, published in 1602. Its poetic merit is slight, like other American epics of the time, a work of ponderous rhyme. Its historical worth is considerable. He describes near a quarter century of Spanish efforts in the Argentine and nearby lands, mostly as eyewitness, filling a large gap in knowledge of that little-known period. He notes Drake's and Cavendish's English piracies, Peru events under Viceroy Toledo, and several violent earthquakes, though not always with correct dates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massa-carrara:
Massa Carrara was a diocese in central Italy's Lunigiana and Garfagnana, seated on the Frigido in a mining district famed above all for pure white marble. Romans preferred it to Paros and Pentelius stone. In the ninth century it belonged to Luni's bishops, confirmed by Otto I and Frederick Barbarossa, though truly subject to the Malaspina counts of Lunigiana.

It passed from Lucca to Pisa, to Visconti and Fieschi, back to Lucca, then stood a free commune under Florence's protection. In 1434 it took Marquis Antonio Alberico Malaspina as lord. In 1548 the marquisate passed to the Cybo house through Lorenzo Cybo's marriage to Riccarda Malaspina, in 1568 Carrara became a principality, and in 1664 a duchy. Alderamo's daughter married Rinaldo Ercole d'Este, joining the duchy to Modena, which regained it after Elisa Bacchiochi in 1806 and Maria Beatrice in 1814.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-megara:
Megara, a titular see under Corinth in Achaia, was built on a dry strip between two rocks, with two ports on the Saronic Gulf and the Gulf of Corinth. In the eighth and seventh centuries B.C. it mothered flourishing colonies: Megara Hyblaea and Selinus in Sicily, Selymbria, Chalcedon, Astacus, Byzantium, and Pontic Heraclea. Pericles' exclusion of Megara from the Attic market in 432 helped spark the Peloponnesian War.

The poor Megarian land was then ravaged year after year, and in 427 Nicias planted a permanent post on Minoa facing Nisaea. Shortly before, Megara had borne the Sophist Eucleides, a disciple of Socrates who founded the Megarian school about 400 B.C., famed for dialectic. The city shared the fate of other Greek towns, and under Anastasius I near the end of the fifth century its walls were restored. Greek and Latin bishops fill the later record in Le Quien and Eubel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miguel-de-cer:
Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra, Spanish author, was born at Alcala de Henares in 1547 and died at Madrid on 23 April 1616. His life story, the article observes, is no less full of interest than the most exciting adventure novel. He received much of his early training at a Madrid school run by the cleric Juan Lopez de Hoyos. He does not seem to have attended any Spanish university.

Like many leading Spanish spirits of his age, he perfected his education by a sojourn in Italy. He then served as a soldier, fought at Lepanto, and endured five years of captivity in Algiers. Returning to Spain, he worked as a tax collector and purchasing agent while writing. His Don Quixote, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615, made him the founder of the modern novel and Spain's greatest literary glory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-military-orde:
The Military Order of Alcantara takes its name from Alcantara, a town on the Tagus, crossed there by a bridge, alcantara in Arabic. It stood in the plain of Estremadura, a great field of conflict between Moslems and Christians in twelfth-century Spain. First taken in 1167 by Fernando II of Leon, Alcantara fell again in 1172 to the Almohad ruler Jussuf, and was recovered only in 1214 by Alfonso of Leon.
