To defend this exposed border conquest, the king turned to military orders, which supplied what the Middle Ages lacked, standing armies and garrisons, combining monastic vows with warfare. The Order of Alcantara, first tied to Calatrava and later independent, guarded the frontier and fought in the Reconquista. It grew rich in lands and commanderies before its incorporation into the Spanish crown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modra:
Modra was an ancient bishop's seat in Asia Minor, now kept only as a titular see. A titular see is a historic diocese with no living bishop, once under the archbishop of Nicaea. This entry traces a place that shows up just once in the classical geographer Strabo. He set it in Phrygia Epicteta near the headwaters of the Gallus river.

Later writers knew the district under shifting names, Medrena and Mela. For a time the town bore the name Justinianopolis Nova in honour of the emperor Justinian. From the twelfth century onward the forms Melagina and Melangeia take over. They point to Malagina, a major staging post for Byzantine armies marching from Constantinople toward Dorylaeum. The entry closes with a roll of its bishops, recorded at church councils from 555 through 1401.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myra:
Myra was a titular see of Lycia in Asia Minor, from time immemorial one of the province's chief places. It stood on the Andriacus river twenty stadia from the sea, with Andriaca as its port. Saint Paul stayed there on his voyage from Caesarea to Rome. The Acts of Paul suggest a Christian community existed there by the second century.

Le Quien opens its bishop list with Saint Nicander, martyred under Domitian about 95. Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker, honoured on 6 December, first appears among Nicaea's fathers in a sixth-century index. Theodosius II made flourishing Myra the capital of Lycia and is said to have built a church to Saint Nicholas there. Bishop Peter later defended Chalcedon in writings quoted by Sophronius and Photius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neutra:
Neutra, or Nitra, is a diocese in Western Hungary, suffragan of Gran, whose exact foundation date is unknown. Some credit Fridigit, wife of a Marcomannic chief, in the mid-fourth century, but without evidence beyond an alleged foundation by Archbishop Wolf of Lorch. It is not a direct continuation of a Svatopluk-era see suffragan of Prague, nor likely King Stephen's foundation.

The see probably arose under King Coloman about 1105 to 1107, though Saint Ladislaus had contemplated it, and a royal document endows Neutra's church with much property. That church, dedicated to Saint Emmeram, stood in Saint Stephen's lifetime and is thought endowed by Queen Gisela. Gervasius was first bishop from 1105 to 1114, followed by Nicholas in 1133. Later kings enriched the see, its chapter grew from nine canons to ten in 1780, and the entry follows its fortunes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-of-l:
Nicholas of Lyra, Doctor planus et utilis, was an exegete born at Lyra in Normandy in 1270 and dead at Paris in 1340. Claims of his Jewish descent first appear only in the fifteenth century. He joined the Franciscans at Verneuil, studied theology, earned his Paris doctorate, and taught at the Sorbonne. In the Beatific Vision dispute he sided with professors against John XXII.

He laboured very successfully, in preaching and writing, for the Jews' conversion, and authored numerous learned works, some still unpublished. Exegesis claimed his best years. In the second prologue to his great Postillae perpetuae in universam Scripturam, he holds the literal sense as the foundation of all mystical reading, alone possessing proving force, as Saint Augustine teaches. He deplores his time's Biblical studies, since careless copyists, unskilled correctors, and the Vulgate's departures from Hebrew obscure the literal sense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nocera:
Nocera in Umbria, a diocese near the Tina's springs famed for mineral waters, guards a tangled early history. Legend makes Crispoldus, a disciple of the apostles, its first bishop, but his Germanic name casts doubt, and the entry separates its bishops from namesakes at Nocera near Naples.

Its first certain bishop, Liutardus, dates to 824, and later prelates restored the cathedral, founded the seminary, and wrote diocesan history. Directly subject to Rome, the diocese counts 82 parishes, nearly 60,000 people, and sixteen religious houses. Antonio Bolognini restored the cathedral in 1438, and Gerolano Maunelli founded the seminary in 1545.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-novara:
Novara, a Piedmontese diocese and manufacturing city, blends Romanesque churches with textile mills. Its cathedral, altered from Romanesque form, holds a high altar by Thorvaldsen and others, a fifth-century baptistery, and archives with codices from the eighth century.

Saint Gaudentius's church, begun in 1553 by Pellegrini, shelters Lombard paintings and frescoes, while the city counts an arts institute and a museum of antiquities. Birthplace of Peter Lombard, Novara passed from counts to bishops under Otto I in 969 and later to dukes and kings. The church of Saint Gaudentius, begun in 1553, replaced an ancient basilica torn down for fortifications.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ogliastra:
Ogliastra, a Sardinian diocese suffragan to Cagliari, was erected by Leo XII in 1824 at King Charles Felix's request. In the Middle Ages, after the Saracens left in 1050, it ranked among five native giudicati, independent districts ruled first by the Sismondi lords.

Its seat, Tortoli, holds about 2,000 people in the Lanusei district, and its first bishop was the Capuchin Serafino Carchero. The diocese counts 29 parishes, 54,500 people, 53 churches and chapels, 46 secular priests, and two schools, one run by Salesians. Its present bishop, Emanuele Virgilio, succeeded Giuseppe Paderi on 15 April 1910, after serving as vicar-general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palmyra:
Palmyra was a titular metropolitan see in Phoenicia Secunda, built by Solomon as Tadmor in the wilderness, though the passage may mean Thamar instead. Long a market town for Romans and Parthians on the caravan road, it kept a Greek constitution, the Seleucid era, the Macedonian calendar, and a Semitic alphabet, speaking an Aramaic dialect. Hadrian visited in 129, and it took the name Hadriana Palmyra.

Septimius Odaenath, prince from 258, called himself king in 260 and took the imperial title in 264. After his death in 267 his widow Zenobia, with ministers Longinus and Paul of Samosata, built an empire, seizing Egypt and part of Asia Minor. Aurelian sacked the city in 272 and carried Zenobia off captive. Diocletian camped a legion there, Justinian restored it, and later wars wore it down.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patara:
Patara was a titular see of Lycia, suffragan of Myra, once a great trading town facing Rhodes. Phoenicians may have founded it, a Dorian colony from Crete followed, and legend traces it to Patarus, son of Apollo. Rich in wealth, it was richer in fame for Apollo's temple, where oracles spoke through winter. Ptolemy Philadelphus enlarged it as Arsinoe. Saint Paul sailed from Patara to Tyre on his third journey.

Bishop lists name it among Myra's suffragans into the thirteenth century. Le Quien names seven bishops, from Eudemus at Nicaea in 325 and Cyrinus at Chalcedon in 451 to Licinius at Constantinople in 536 and Theodulus at the Photian council in 879. Saint Methodius, sometimes listed here, more likely belonged to Olympus. Ruins near Djelemish show a theatre of Antoninus Pius, Vespasian baths, temples, tombs, and a sand-choked port.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-de-riba:
Pedro de Ribadeneira was a Spanish Jesuit remembered chiefly as a writer and historian of his order. Born at Toledo in 1526, he went to Italy as a page in Cardinal Farnese's household. He joined the Society of Jesus at fourteen, days before its papal approval. His studies took him to Paris, Louvain, and Padua, and he taught rhetoric at Palermo.

His later career mixed diplomacy, preaching, and administration across Europe. He sought recognition for the Society in the Low Countries, preached at Louvain and Brussels, and spent months in London during Mary Tudor's final illness. Ill health sent him back to Spain, where he wrote for his last decades. His eyewitness Life of St. Ignatius, a history of the English schism, and the popular Flos sanctorum crowned that work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-martyr-:
Peter Martyr d'Anghiera was an Italian humanist who became Spain's historian of discovery, born at Arona on Lake Maggiore in 1457. He reached Rome at twenty, won patrons among the cardinals, and followed the Count of Tendilla to Saragossa in 1487. Soon he lectured at Salamanca and taught young nobles at the Spanish court, where Castile's best minds sat at his feet. In 1501 he carried a diplomatic mission to Egypt's sultan.

His fame rests on the Decades, eight books drawing on Columbus's letters, discoverers' tales, and council reports, from Caribbean shores to Cortés's march. He first grasped the Gulf Stream's meaning, and his lively narratives remain a prime source for the geography of discovery. All eight Decades appeared together at Alcalá in 1530, with his 812 letters, the Opus epistolarum, the same year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petra:
Petra was the rock city of the Nabataeans, a titular metropolitan see of Palaestina Tertia. Scripture calls the place Sela, the Rock, an eagle's nest on a mountain top, where King Amaziah of Jerusalem dashed 10,000 Edomite captives from a cliff in the ninth century BC. It was then a refuge of caves rather than Edom's capital, which stood at Bosra.

By the fourth century BC Arab merchants called Nabataeans held it, growing rich as middlemen between Arabia, Egypt, and Syria. Antigonus's general Athenaeus seized it by surprise in 312 BC, and later it became metropolis of Palaestina Salutaris, taking Hadrian's name after his visit. Christianity came early, bishops like Asterius defended Nicaea, and monks flourished there. Trade shifted, Palmyra rose, and Petra fell to ruin, leaving over 3,000 rock tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pinara:
Pinara was a leading city of the Lycian confederation in Asia Minor and later a titular see, a former bishopric kept in name. It is said to have been founded by Pinarus with early Cretan settlers, or as a colony called Artymnessus. It took its name from the Lycian word for round hill, matching the hill on which it stood.

Now the village of Minara in the Konya region, it keeps splendid ruins: walls, a theatre, an acropolis, rock tombs, and rare Lycian inscriptions, with remains of a church. Five of its bishops are known, from Eustathius at Seleucia in 359 to Athanasius at the Photian Council of Constantinople in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polidoro-da-c:
Polidoro da Caravaggio, born Caldara at Caravaggio in 1492 or 1495, was an Italian painter who rose from carrying mortar to serving Raphael. He left home at eighteen in poverty and reached Rome, where he hauled plaster for the Vatican fresco painters. Watching them copy Raphael's designs, he learned so fast that Raphael took him as a pupil.

He studied antiquity and became the first Roman master to use chiaroscuro, the play of light and shade, with colour secondary. He adorned Roman palace fronts in sgraffito, designs scratched through a light layer over dark stucco, now known only from engravings. After the sack of Rome in 1527 he worked at Naples and Messina, where his Christ Bearing the Cross of 1534 stands as his masterpiece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prefecture-ap:
Sumatra prefecture was raised by a Decree of 30 June 1911 and given to the Dutch Capuchins. Ere that it belonged to Batavia's Vicariate Apostolic, under Holland's Jesuits. The new prefecture covers Sumatra and nearby isles, counting Bangka, of 4,888 square miles and 78,000 folk. Sumatra, Ptolemy's Jabadin, visited by Marco Polo in 1292, was found by the Portuguese navigator Siqueira in 1508 and held by the Dutch from 1599. It spans about 181,000 square miles.

The entry calls the natives indolent and cruel. Their faith mixes fetishism and Mahommedanism. At the start of 1911 the Jesuits held four chief mission centres and sixteen lesser stations: Medan, Padang, Koata Radja, and Tandjeong-Sakti. The Sisters of Charity of Tilburg stood at Padang. Two mission schools served, and Catholics numbered 4,600, of whom 3,200 were Europeans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quem-terra-po:
Quem Terra, Pontus, Sidera is an ancient hymn honouring the Blessed Virgin. This encyclopedia entry weighs its authorship with care. Thomasius and Mone ascribe it to Fortunatus without question, but also without giving a reason. Kayser objects that the hymn never appears in manuscripts of Fortunatus's works. Dreves and Blume still refer it to him, and the entry leaves the question open rather than settling it.

The Roman Breviary splits the hymn in two. The first part, opening with Quem terra, pontus, sidera, serves at Matins in the Common Office and in the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin. The second, opening O gloriosa virginum, serves at Lauds. Both close with the Marian doxology Jesu tibi sit gloria. Both parts revise, in stricter classical metre, the older hymn Quem terra, pontus, aethera, found in many old breviaries and in manuscripts of great age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rafael-carrer:
Rafael Carrera, born in Guatemala on 24 October 1814 and dead there on 14 April 1865, ranks among the most remarkable men Central America has produced. This encyclopedia entry stresses his humble start: a mestizo with no chance of schooling, he could sign his name only once he had already risen to power. The usual verdict paints him as a cruel, bloodthirsty upstart from the lowest ranks, hostile to liberty, progress and even order.

That last charge is certainly false. Carrera brought order to the bloody chaos into which factions had plunged Guatemala for decades. Two parties tore Central America apart: the Centralists, holding to Spanish colonial traditions, and the Federalists, dreaming of a federation of the Central American states after the United States. Strife had raged between them for years, and towards his life's end Carrera still had to crush attempts at insurrection, so firmly did he hold the country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhinocolura:
Rhinocolura was a titular see in Augustamnica Prima, suffragan of Pelusium, and a maritime town on the boundary of Egypt and Palestine, claimed by geographers for one country or the other. Its history is unknown. Diodorus Siculus tells a founding legend: Actisanes, King of Ethiopia, settled there criminals with their noses cut off, a tale invented to give the town's name a Greek meaning.

Strabo calls it the former great emporium for the merchandise of India and Arabia, unloaded at Leuce Come on the Red Sea's eastern shore and carried via Petra to Rhinocolura. It is usually identified with the present fortified village of El Anish, with four hundred inhabitants besides the garrison, half a mile from the sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salvete-chris:
Salvete Christi Vulnera, Hail wounds of Christ, is the Roman Breviary hymn at Lauds, morning prayer, for the feast of the Most Precious Blood. Found in the appendix to the spring part of the Breviary printed at Venice in 1798, the office had served since 1735 as a Lenten commemoration in some dioceses. There it was kept on the Friday after the fourth Sunday of Lent. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gives the hymn's history in brief.

Pius IX added the feast to the regular Breviary on 10 August 1849, setting it for the first Sunday of July. Faber read the timing, just after the pope's return from Gaeta, as a perpetual thanksgiving for a deliverance. Eight stanzas in Ambrosian iambic dimeter verse, with a doxology praising the Father's right hand and the Spirit's strength, make up the hymn. A cento, or patchwork, of stanzas one, two, four, and eight serves another office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-cruz-de:
Santa Cruz de la Sierra, a Bolivian diocese erected on 6 July 1605 as suffragan of Lima, has depended on La Plata since 1609. It covers the departments of Santa Cruz and Beni, west of Brazil's Mato Grosso. Its first bishop was Antonio Calderón. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia centres on the Moxos missions.

The wooded lowlands are home to the Moxos Indians, among whom Jesuits under Cipriano Baraza built flourishing seventeenth-century missions. Over 50,000 converts were counted when the Society was suppressed, after which the missions fell fast, though many Moxos remain fervent Catholics today. The town of Santa Cruz, 18,000 strong and founded in 1575 on the Piray river, anchors a diocese of about 250,000 Catholics, 103 priests, fifty-four parishes, and seventy-four churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sara:
Sara, Hebrew for princess, called Sarai before Genesis chapter seventeen, was Abraham's wife and also his half-sister. No other account of her parentage survives. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows the Genesis story, with its doublings noted rather than smoothed away.

Fleeing famine to Egypt, Abraham had Sara, still beautiful at sixty-five, pass as his sister, and Egypt's king took her as wife until a divine warning restored her. A variant tale repeats the pattern with Abimelech of Gerar. Barren until ninety, Sara bore Isaac as promised, then, jealous of her maid Hagar the Egyptian, who had borne Abraham a son, she forced Abraham to send Hagar and Ishmael away.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sauatra:
Sauatra, a titular see of Lycaonia suffragan of Iconium, has no known town history, though its coins survive and Strabo, Ptolemy, Hierocles, and the Peutinger Table all mention it. Its name is spelled as on the coins; Sabatra matches it in sound, and Strabo gives Soatra. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia pins a lost town to a road and two bishops.

The town stood in dry country on the road from Laodicea to Archelais, near modern Souverek in Konya province, by one account four hours south-west of Eskil. Le Quien names two bishops: Aristophanes, present at Constantinople's first ecumenical council in 381, and Eustathius, alive at Chalcedon in 451. Greek lists mention the see until the thirteenth century, and the entry leaves its exact site open between rival guesses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silveira:
Gonçalo da Silveira, pioneer missionary of South Africa, was born at Almeirim near Lisbon on 23 February 1526 and martyred on 6 March 1561. Tenth child of Dom Luis da Silveira, first Count of Sortelha, he lost his parents in infancy and was raised by his sister Philippa and her husband, the Marquis of Tavora. Schooled by Franciscans until 1542, he finished studies at Coimbra, where after little more than a year he was received into the Society of Jesus.

Appointed provincial of India in 1555, with Ignatius's approval shortly before the founder's death, he governed three years as a worthy successor of Francis Xavier. A hundred Jesuits under him labored with much success, though he owned himself unsuited to government, lacking tact with human weakness. The entry's later chapters follow his mission to the Monomotapa kingdom, where he won the king's favor before jealous rivals brought about his martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sonora:
Sonora was a Mexican diocese matching the state of the same name, suffragan to Durango, and this entry sketches its land, people, and mission history. Covering 76,619 square miles with 262,545 inhabitants in 1910, it was governed from Hermosillo, where both bishop and state governor resided.

The Gospel first reached the region with Father Niza and the early Spanish explorers. And Jesuits later built the famed missions of the Yaqui and Mayo rivers and of Upper and Lower Pimeria, among them the celebrated Father Kino. After the Jesuits were expelled from the Spanish colonies in 1767, the missions passed to other hands, and the entry follows that handover as part of northern Mexico's Catholic story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sora:
Sora was a small titular see in Paphlagonia, suffragan to Gangra, whose exact site was fixed only by an inscription found at the village of Zorah. The entry notes the local era and the worship of Zeus Epicarpios recorded there. And places the town later under the Praetor of Paphlagonia, with mentions in Constantine Porphyrogenitus and the Greek lists of bishoprics down to the thirteenth century.

Le Quien names six of its bishops, from Theodore, represented at Chalcedon in 451, through Olympius, John, Theophanes, Phocas. And Constantine, each tied to a great council of the early Church. For a town the entry calls insignificant, Sora leaves a surprisingly clear trail through the councils that shaped Christian doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-afra:
St. Afra was a martyr of Augsburg, in the Roman province of Rhaetia, and this entry separates firm fact from later legend. Augusta Vindelicorum, now Augsburg, stood on the Lech near the Danube, a colony given municipal rights by Hadrian, where Christianity had arrived before Constantine, as Afra's martyrdom itself proves.

It is certain history, the entry insists, that a Christian named Afra was beheaded at Augsburg under Diocletian about 304 for steadfast profession of faith. And that her grave drew great veneration early. The Hieronymian Martyrology, compiled from fourth-century calendars, lists her on 5 August, with some manuscripts giving 6 or 7 August, and the entry builds its case on those early witnesses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-barbara:
St. Barbara was a virgin and martyr whose name appears in no authentic early historical authority for Christian antiquity. This entry follows the legend that filled that gap. Her name does not appear in the original recension of St. Jerome's martyrology. Veneration of her was common, however, from the seventh century. By about that date legendary Acts of her martyrdom existed, inserted in Symeon Metaphrastes's collection and used by the authors of enlarged ninth-century martyrologies in Western Europe.

Those narratives agree in essentials: Barbara was the daughter of Dioscorus, a rich heathen. Her father guarded her carefully, keeping her shut up in a tower to preserve her from the outside world. An offer of marriage received through him she rejected. Before going on a journey, her father ordered a bath-house to be built, and the entry follows the legend from there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-mura:
Mura, an Irish abbot of the seventh century, presided over Fahan in Donegal and left relics still treasured today. Born in County Donegal about 550, St Columba made him abbot of Fahan, and the monastery took his name after his death. He stood high in the regard of Hugh, high king of Ireland, and wrote chronicles plus a rhymed life of Columba quoted in the Martyrology of Donegal.

He is counted special patron of the O'Neill clan, sixth in descent from its founder, whose name lives on in Inishowen. He died about 645, and his feast falls on 12 March. His crozier rests in the National Museum at Dublin, his bell-shrine in the Wallace Collection, and a carved cross and holy well mark his church at Fahan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nicholas-o:
Nicholas of Myra, also called Nicholas of Bari, counts among the most popular saints of East and West, though little about him is historically certain. The entry is firm on one point only: he was bishop of Myra in Lycia in the fourth century, dying on 6 December 345 or 352. Legend adds a pilgrimage to Egypt and Palestine, imprisonment under Diocletian, and presence at Nicaea.

That last claim is doubted, since his name appears in no old list of Nicaea's bishops. In 1087 Italian merchants carried his body from Myra to Bari, and his cult spread through Italy, Germany, and Russia. Justinian built him a church at Constantinople in the sixth century. Readers learn to separate a beloved legend from a thin historical core.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-of-a:
Peter of Alcantara, a Spanish Franciscan reformer, led the Discalced movement with extreme austerity. Born at Alcántara in 1499 to the town governor Peter Garavita, he studied grammar and philosophy at home, then went to Salamanca at fourteen. He joined the Stricter Observance Franciscans in 1515 and founded a new community at Badajoz at twenty-two.

Ordained in 1524, he preached chiefly to the poor, drawing sermons from the Prophets and wisdom books with tender sympathy. As minister of St Gabriel's province he drew up constitutions at Plasencia in 1540, resigned under opposition, and pressed on with reform in Spain and Portugal. He died on 18 October 1562, famed for penance and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-theodotus-:
Theodotus of Ancyra, an innkeeper martyr, turned his house into a refuge, hospital, and church under persecution. The Roman Martyrology for 18 May names him with his aunt Thecusa and the virgins Alexandra, Claudia, Faina, Euphrasia, Matrona, and Julitta. He has a special feast on 7 June and serves as patron of innkeepers, with torches and sword as emblems.

A married man keeping an inn at Ancyra, capital of Galatia, he was zealous in Christian duties and charity to neighbours. He brought sinners to repentance and strengthened many during the persecution of Governor Theoctenus about 303 under Diocletian's edict. When provisions had first to be offered to idols, he stocked his house and sheltered Christians, nursed the sick, and buried the martyred virgins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stefano-infes:
Stefano Infessura, a Roman lawyer and chronicler, wrote the Diary of the City of Rome from 1294 to 1494. Born at Rome about 1435, he studied law, took a doctorate, and gained solid legal knowledge. He served as judge at Orte, then came to Rome's university as professor of Roman law. Under Sixtus IV his office suffered when the pope withheld university income and cut professors' salaries.

Infessura also served long as secretary of the Roman Senate. He was entangled in Stefano Porcaro's conspiracy against Nicholas V in 1453, aiming to overthrow papal government and make Rome a republic. He also belonged to the antipapal faction among the paganising humanists of Pomponio Leto's Roman Academy. His Diary holds little value before Martin V and Eugene IV, but grows into a vivid source for late fifteenth-century Rome. He died about 1500.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sura:
Sura was a titular see in Augusta Euphratensis, suffragan of Hierapolis, standing on the Euphrates where roads from Palmyra and Beroea met. A military station, it housed the prefect of the Sixteenth Flavian Legion early in the fifth century. In his second Syrian campaign, Chosroes attacked the town, whose defence the Armenian general Arsaces directed until he fell.

The townspeople then sent their bishop to Chosroes as envoy, but the king, angered by resistance, ordered the town destroyed, though it had held out only half an hour. Justinian later raised strong fortifications there. Three bishops are known, from Chalcedon in 451, exile as a Monophysite in 518, and the unnamed envoy, and the see appears in Antioch's lists of the sixth and tenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syra:
Syra is a Latin diocese, suffragan of Naxos, covering the Cycladic island of Syra in the Aegean. About thirty-one square miles with 32,000 people, the island was first called Syria, was settled by Phoenicians, and was home in legend to Eumaeus the swineherd and to Pherecydes, teacher of Pythagoras. It played no great role in antiquity and at first had no bishop at all.

Venetians conquered it definitively in 1207 and held it until Barbarossa took it for the Turks in 1522, and it joined the Greek kingdom after 1821. A Latin bishopric under Athens, then Naxos, dates from Venetian rule, and its most famed holder, John Andrew Carga, was strangled by Turks in 1617 for refusing Islam. Greek metropolitans appear from the Turkish period onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tabbora: Tabbora, also called Talbora, was a titular see in Africa Proconsularis, suffragan of Carthage. It is identified with two nearby groups of ruins now called Tembra, west of Bijga in the Wady Siliana valley of Tunis. Only two bishops are known. Marinus attended the Conference of Carthage in 411 against a rival named Victor. Constantine signed the province's letter to Patriarch Paul of Constantinople against the Monothelites in 646.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teuchira: Teuchira, or Teucheira, was a titular see in Libyan Pentapolis. This city on Cyrenaica's coast stood 200 stadia west of Ptolemais. It was famed for worship of Cybele, honoured with annual festivals. Under the Ptolemies it was called Arsinoë, later it became a Roman colony, and Justinian garrisoned it. Its ruins are called Tokra in the vilayet of Benghasi. Two bishops are known: Secundus at Nice in 325 and Zeno at Ephesus in 431. The see appears in Parthey's list about 840.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thagora:
Thagora, or Tagora, was a titular see in Numidia, called Thacora in the Peutinger Table and mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary. Justinian fortified it. Today it is the village of Taoura, near Ain Guettar, about thirteen miles southeast of Souk Ahras, ancient Thagaste, in Constantine department, Algeria. It holds ruins of baths, a church, and Justinian's fortress, with many inscriptions found. Thagura was the birthplace of St Crispin, martyred at Theveste under Diocletian, whose feast falls on 5 December.

Sts Julius and Potamia and ten other martyrs also died there, and the Roman martyrology commemorates them on the same day. Three bishops of Thagura are known: Kanthippus in 401, named in a letter of St Augustine, Restitutus at the Conference of Carthage in 411, and Timotheus, exiled by Huneric in 484. The entry closes with Toulotte and Diehl on Christian Numidia and Byzantine Africa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-themiscyra:
Amazon country on the Thermodon's mouth gives this titular see its romance, suffragan of Amasea in the Hellespont. Herodotus and most classical authors mention the town near modern Therme-Tchai. Scylax calls it Greek, Diodorus an Amazonian foundation, and mythology made the region the warrior women's native land. Ptolemy still lists it, though Mela and Strabo pass the town in silence.

Lucullus besieged it after Mithridates withdrew from Cyzicus, and inhabitants defended it with courage. Destruction likely followed, since Strabo praises the country of Themiscyra at length while ignoring its town. Not in the episcopal lists of Le Quien, it lay near present Therme on the Black Sea, in a land counted among the world's richest and most beautiful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-abuc:
Bishop Theodore Abucara of Caria in Syria, who died probably in 770, earns this brief entry for his anti-heretical dialogues. In them he often claimed to reproduce the very words of John of Damascus, the great Eastern theologian whose disciple he was. John's three famous discourses defending sacred images were addressed to him.

Scholars have tried to identify Abucara with a Bishop Theodore of Caria who attended Constantinople's Eighth Ecumenical Council in 869, nearly a century after his probable death. The entry, citing Marin's dictionary article, leaves the identification open, a small puzzle in Byzantine theology's history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-o-ha:
Kentucky poet Theodore O'Hara, author of The Bivouac of the Dead, is the soldier-writer remembered here. Born at Danville, Kentucky, on 11 February 1822, dying at Guerryton, Alabama, on 6 June 1867, he was son of Kane O'Hara, Irish political exile turned prominent Kentucky educator. Saint Joseph's College, Bardstown, and law study preceded Mexican War service to brevet major.

Filibustering expeditions to Cuba and Central America, newspaper editing, and government diplomatic missions followed. Civil War staff service under Generals Johnson and Breckenridge closed his public career. Little of special merit survives beyond two poems, Bivouac and Dirge for the Brave Old Pioneer, the former's opening stanza lines inscribed over Arlington National Cemetery's entrance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thera:
Volcanic island Thera, or Santorino, in the Cyclades, is the diocese whose fiery past fills this entry. About 2000 before Christ the dead volcano woke, wiped out the people, and sank part of the island in the sea. Eruptions followed: Theresa split off in 236 before Christ, Hiera rose in 196, Thia appeared in 46 after Christ then sank, and new islands rose in 1573, 1711, and 1866.

Ancient Thera town, found at Hagios Stephanos near Mesavouno, held a Ptolemaic garrison. Phoenicians repeopled Calliste after the great blast, Dorians renamed it Thera about 620 before Christ, and Sparta, Athens, Ptolemies, and Rome ruled it in turn. Christians likely came in the second century. Bishops, rites, and the modern diocese close a tale written in ash and sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-de-val:
Thomas de Vallgornera, a Dominican theologian born in Catalonia about 1595, wrote one of the classic works of mystical theology. A member of the Barcelona convent, he served as its vicar-general while Catalonia stood under French rule around 1642. His Mystica Theologia D. Thomae first appeared at Barcelona in 1662, with an enlarged edition three years later.

The book sets out the mystical teaching of Thomas Aquinas, arguing that true mysticism must rest on sound scholastic doctrine or it drifts into error. Long rare, it was reissued at Turin in 1890 by Father Berthier, who kept the 1662 text in the body and moved the 1665 additions to an appendix. Vallgornera died in September 1665.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thyatira:
Thyatira was a city of Lydia, in Asia Minor, and a titular suffragan see of Sardes. Its name may come from Seleucus I, though a Lydian origin is more likely. A Macedonian colony settled there, and its people worshipped Asclepius, Bacchus, Artemis and above all Apollo, with games in his honour. Vespasian built there, and Hadrian visited in 123 and Caracalla in 215.

Lydia, the woman converted by Paul at Philippi, came from Thyatira, and John's Revelation addresses its church, praising it while rebuking a false prophetess. By the early third century almost the whole city was Christian, says Epiphanius. Its bishops include Seras in 325 and Fuscus at Ephesus in 431. Under the Turks it became Ak-Hissar, the white fortress, a town of 22,000 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiara:
The tiara is the papal crown, a costly beehive-shaped covering set with stones and pearls, topped by a small cross and ringed with three royal diadems. From those three crowns it is also called the triregnum. It is not a liturgical ornament: the pope wears a mitre at liturgical functions and reserves the tiara for processions, solemn entries and acts of jurisdiction such as dogmatic decisions.

First named as camelaucum in the life of Pope Constantine, who reigned from 708 to 715, it grew through three stages. At first it bore no royal circlet, then one, then two under Boniface VIII, whose lifetime statues show the double crown. Three crowns appear first in an inventory of the papal treasure dated 1315 or 1316, marking the tiara's final form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-titus-bishop-:
Titus, Bishop of Bostra, was born about 362 to 371 and counted by Sozomen among the great men of Constantius's reign. Julian the Apostate tried a mean trick on him: fearing riots when paganism returned, Julian warned Titus that he and his clergy would answer for any outbreak. Titus replied that the Christians, though equal in number to the pagans, would keep quiet.

Julian then wrote to the Bostrians urging them to expel Titus. He claimed Titus had slandered them, crediting their calm to his influence rather than their own temper. Titus later signed the Antioch synod's letter to Jovian in 363, accepting the Nicene Creed with a clause softening homoousios. Jerome praises his mighty books against the Manichaeans and his secular learning, and he followed the literal Antiochene way of reading Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tommaso-maria:
Tommaso Maria Zigliara, cardinal, theologian and philosopher, was born at Bonifacio, Corsica, late in October 1833 and died at Rome in 1893. Baptized Francesco, he studied classics at home under the Jesuit Aloysius Piras. He joined the Dominicans at Rome at eighteen, and was ordained at Perugia in May 1856 by Cardinal Pecci, the future Leo XIII.

He taught philosophy at Rome, Corbara and Viterbo, served as master of novices, and became regent of the Minerva college in Rome. When the Italian government seized the Minerva convent in 1873, he carried on lectures with the Fathers of the Holy Ghost at the French College until a house nearby was found. Bishops from France, Italy, Germany, England and America sought his counsel, and his fame as a teacher spread widely through Rome and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Portugal's university story begins with certain evidence from 1288, when the Abbot of Alcobaça, several priors, and parish priests told Nicholas IV of their plan. King Diniz had granted them a Studium Generale at Lisbon, and they had agreed to pay the doctors and masters from monastery and church revenues. They begged the pope to confirm the bargain and protect a work begun for God's service and their country's glory.

A bull dated 9 August 1290, sent to Lisbon's university of masters and students, saw the pope agree to the plan and welcome the new seat of studies. The bull sanctioned taxation of lodgings in the Paris and Bologna fashion. The entry follows the studium through its moves between Lisbon and Coimbra, its royal patrons, and its growth into Portugal's historic university, long settled at Coimbra.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-antonio-m:
Antonio Maria Claret y Clara was a Spanish prelate and missionary, born at Sallent near Barcelona on 23 December 1807, who died at Fontfroide near Narbonne on 24 October 1870. Son of a small woollen manufacturer, he learned his letters in his village and became a weaver at twelve. Later he went to Barcelona to master his trade, staying until twenty, while spare hours gave him Latin, French, and engraving, plus a spell as an army volunteer.

Sensing a call to a higher life, he departed Barcelona, joined the Vich seminary in 1829, and took ordination on 13 June 1835. After a benefice in his home parish and further theology study, he wished to become a Carthusian, but mission preaching drew him more strongly. The entry follows his missions across Catalonia, his founding of the Claretians, and his years as Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
The Sahara vicariate covers a desert some 932 miles north to south and 2,484 miles east to west, dotted with oases that form its centres of population. Eight years after Duveyrier's scientifically important journey of 1859 to 1861, Pius IX appointed Archbishop Lavigerie of Algiers delegate apostolic of the Sahara and Sudan in 1868.

Jesuits settled at Laghouat that year, urging dispensaries and schools, and White Fathers replaced them in 1872, spreading to Biskra, Ouargla, Touggourt, and Ghardaïa. Two attempts to cross the desert to Timbuktu, a great slave market, aimed to join the struggle against slavery. The first, in December 1878, ended with Fathers Ménoret, Paulmier. Bouchard slain by their Tuareg guides, the White Fathers' first martyrs, whose beatification cause opened at Rome in 1909.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-volterra:
Volterra is a Tuscan diocese whose city stands on a rocky mountain 1,770 feet above sea level, between the Bra and Cecina rivers, ringed by strong walls. Its cathedral, consecrated by Callistus II in 1120 and enlarged by Andrea Pisano in 1254 and again in 1576, holds sculpture by Mino da Fiesole, an Annunciation by Luca Signorelli.

Pictures by Benvenuto di Giovanni and Leonardo da Pistoia, while its 1283 baptistery holds a font by Sansovino. Other landmarks include St Lino and St Francis churches, the Palazzo Pubblico of 1217 with the city archives, the Palazzo Tagani's museum of Etruscan and Roman antiquities. A citadel built in 1343 by the Duke of Athens and enlarged by Florence. Ancient walls, baths, an aqueduct, an amphitheatre, and above all Etruscan burial places survive nearby. The district thrives on alabaster working, mineral waters, boric acid from Larderello's soffioni, and the baths of Montecatini.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zamora:
Zamora is the vicariate apostolic in south Ecuador, created 3 February 1893 by Leo XIII. The second Quito provincial council of 1869 set up a mission for the region's savages with four chief houses at Napo, Macas, Gualaquiza, and Zamora. Jesuits ran it, though rebel tribes badly hampered their work. In 1889 the Franciscans took over Zamora, and at the end of 1892 Father Luis Torra settled among savages numbering seven hundred to a thousand. He faced harsh resistance to settled communal life as he worked among them.

Its name comes from an earlier Spanish settlement razed in 1559. Its country is beautiful, its fertile plains watered by fine rivers, yet recent savage revolts have driven missionaries back to the Franciscan convent at Loja.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zara:
Zara is the Dalmatian archdiocese, a diocese since A.D. 381 and an archdiocese since 1146, with eighty bishops in unbroken succession. Bishop Sabinianus appears in Gregory the Great's Register, and John VIII names Saint Donatus as patron of Jadera, Zara's ancient name. Archaeologists find Germanic ecclesiastical sculpture from the tribal migrations there. The Church of Saint Donatus, its rotunda dome ringed by a two-story vaulted gallery around three eastern apses, is Dalmatia's finest structure of its period.

Zara was Byzantine Dalmatia's capital, yet its Carolingian architecture shows it once belonged to the Franks, explaining Bishop Donatus's visit to Charlemagne at Dietenhofen. Ægidius of Viterbo, who governed two years, told the Fifth Lateran Council that men must be changed by what is holy, not what is holy by men. He warned Julius II that the Church's weapons are faith, virtue, and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zoara:
Zoara is the Palestina Tertia titular see, the ancient Bala or Segor, one of the Pentapolis's five cities, which escaped the thunder and lightning for sheltering Lot and his family. Josephus, Ptolemy, and Eusebius and Saint Jerome in the Onomasticon all mention it.

Bishops ascribed to Zoara include Musonius at Ephesus in 449 and Chalcedon in 451, Isidore in 518, and John in 536. At the fourth century's end one of its bishops accompanied the western pilgrim wrongly named Silvia. The pseudo-Antoninus in the sixth century describes its monks and extols its palm trees. During the French occupation it took the name Palmer or Paumier. William of Tyre, Foulcher of Chartres, and Arab geographers all praise its dates. It is not known when the city vanished; traces may lie in Ghor-es-Safieh at Wadi el-Qrahy's mouth.
cleopatra:
H. Rider Haggard dedicated this novel to his mother in January 1889 and wrote it as the life story of Harmachis, an Egyptian prince and priest of Isis. Harmachis is bred from childhood for one task: to free Egypt from foreign rule and take revenge on the queen, Cleopatra. Haggard uses the priest's own narration to explain the great mystery of the queen's flight at Actium.

Harmachis reaches the court, wins the queen's trust, and finds his sworn duty at war with his fascination. The tale runs through conspiracy, betrayal, and ruin to Cleopatra's death, which Haggard argues came by poison rather than the famous asp. Ancient rites, temple secrets, and a traitor's remorse fill the space between the history the reader already knows.
